May I say I am very pleased indeed to see you sitting in the chair at the moment, and as we come to the end of the session I recognize that you have been diverted to other important matters during the course of the session which have not gone unnoticed by hon. members.
I too, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, am very happy that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, who is momentarily out of the chamber, chose to participate in this debate. When the hon. member for Okan-agan-Revelstoke spoke about an hour ago 79951-0-4624
Supply-Labour
I expressed not only my pleasure in his participation but in his contribution. Those of us in the opposition who have the responsibility of scrutinizing government policy welcome whatever help we can get from hon. members who sit behind the ministry, particularly when their observations are of an objective kind, in keeping with the high standards of objective scrutiny which we in the Liberal party endeavour to maintain toward these important matters.
I also join with the hon. member who has just taken his seat in paying tribute to the personnel in the unemployment insurance commission, the commission itself, the officers in Ottawa and those in the various offices in the country. I should like in a special way to pay tribute to the personnel of the unemployment insurance commission offices in my own city of Windsor, who have been faced with a very heavy responsibility arising out of the high level of unemployment that has prevailed there during the past three years. I am sure that the citizens of Windsor generally are grateful and would want me to say to the minister that there is much appreciation by industry, by the unions and by the citizens generally of the devotion to service of the personnel in the Windsor office.
The manager of the Windsor office, Mr. John Sharrer, is to retire some time within the course of the next four or five months, I understand. I do not know the exact time, but I understand that his retirement is imminent. I should like to say that Mr. Sharrer has been a devoted public servant. He has sought to inform the public of his responsibilities, of the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and he has contributed in no small measure to whatever alleviation of the problem of unemployment was at his disposal.
I am happy to say this, because when he was appointed I felt that the direction of that office should go to someone who resided in the city of Windsor. Of course the appointment was not at the disposal of the government of the day; it was a matter that rested as the minister knows, with the civil service commission. But I felt that where possible the procedures of the civil service commission ought to recognize local talent. Nevertheless, the fact is that this gentleman has performed a notable service, I want to pay him this inadequate but well deserved tribute.
The unemployment insurance administration has to do not only with the granting of benefits to those who have legal entitlement, but with the administration of a very large operation. It is the custodian of large sums of money, contributed to mainly by the two principal contributors, the employees and the employers, with the federal government contributing a much smaller amount. When one

Supply-Labour
considers the criticism that was levelled at the unemployment insurance scheme, when first established, one wonders whether criticisms that are directed toward social legislation take into account the actual achievements of such measures when they are put to full use. In this period of high unemployment, where would we be but for the unemployment insurance act and the unemployment insurance fund? I am sure it is the concern of all of us that the fund be maintained in such proportions as to always be able to provide the contractual benefits which exist as a result of the arrangements made among the beneficiaries, the contributors and the state.
The concern that is now in my mind is that if the prognostications concerning unemployment in the ensuing period are valid, the fund is going to be tested in the next 12 months as it has not been tested since the act first came into being in 1941. The government, I am sure, has been giving consideration to this matter. The government, I am sure, has been giving consideration to the definite possibility, that it will be called on to replenish the fund. Notwithstanding the fact that last year it increased the contributions of the employers and employees, the revenue was estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $75 million to $78 million, although I understand the actual revenues were not as great as anticipated. If I am wrong in that connection the minister will possibly indicate the extent of the inaccuracy. These increases in contributions were imposed without changing the basic pattern of benefits. In spite of the increases in revenues, the fund continues to be in a precarious state.
The Minister of Labour was asked by the hon. member for Gloucester, early this session, what amount was to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund on June 30, 1957, 1958, 1959 and 1960. The minister replied to this question on July 27 last. He indicated in that reply that as of June 30, 1957, the fund stood at $852,729,261.78; as of June 30, 1958, at $644,520,634.54; as of June 30, 1959, $434,152,690.64; as of June 30, 1960, $296,187,477.10. I direct the attention of the committee to the drop from 1957 to the present time. The present level of the fund, on the basis of this return, which I believe is not the final word in the matter, nevertheless reflects the seriousness of the state of the fund at the present time. Unless the government can show a greater potential revenue than we have thus far had in the experience of the fund's operation, if we have a comparable level of unemployment there will not be enough money in the fund to provide the benefits acquired by right by those who, being

out of work, require this particular form of assistance in order to provide for themselves and their families.
This is, of course, a serious matter, but I do not believe the problem can be allowed to rest at the figure given for June 30, 1960. I have in my hand the unemployment insurance commission report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959, the last available report. I direct the committee's attention to page 25, where under the title "Claims", the report presents the following:
The increase in the volume of initial claims which commenced, towards the end of 1957-
The words "end of 1957", should be underlined.
-continued until October 1958, resulting in a record number of initial claims being filed.
Then on page 31 of the report, in the second complete paragraph under the title "Unemployment Insurance Fund", we find this:
Benefit payments during 1958-59 amounted to $478,631,077.67. Revenue from all sources amounted to $234,242,110.31.
I jump over the next sentence, which is not relevant to my point, and I quote:
The excess of benefit payments over revenue was $244,388,967.36. This left a balance in the fund at the end of the fiscal year of $499,811,157.51. Benefit payments exceeded revenue in all months except August, September and October.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this cannot and must not be allowed to escape our attention. On April 23 last, the Minister of Labour-his words will be found at page 3009 of Hansard -told us the unemployment insurance fund had incurred a financial loss of more than $10 million during the fiscal year 1958-59 as a result of the sale by the commission, under the authority of the investment committee, of government bonds. The committee, of course, will recall that under the act, the investment committee is made up of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the deputy ministers of finance and labour. We know that during the fiscal year 1959-60 and the first two months of this year, another $10 million was lost by the fund, as a result of the sale of government bonds. These two losses in these two different fiscal years were actual losses. I am not now talking, although I will, about the unrealized or book losses.
In any event, these two actual losses represent very impressive amounts, particularly when we take into account the nature of the fund, a fund made up, as I said, of contributions from employees and employers each amounting to more than 80 per cent of the fund, while the contribution of the state is less than 20 per cent of the fund. We refer to this fund not as a government account. It should be regarded for what it is, a trust

account. We should remember that the amount of cash in the fund or the amount of securities in the fund belongs not to the state, but to the workers, to industry, and only a very small part to the government, representing the taxpayers of Canada.
Of the $20 million which was lost as a result of the sale of government bonds and securities during the last two years, more than $16 million was owned by the workers and industry and less than $4 million came from the state. If the loss of $20 million incurred by the fund during the last two years had been due to unmanageable factors, there would be no justification for criticizing the investment policy of the fund. However, I contend that the $20 million loss could and should have been avoided, if there had been the kind of management of that fund which I believe in the case of a trust fund must exist, because of the high obligation imposed on trustees of resources which belong to those who have no manageable control in the fund itself.
Until the end of 1957 there was no real incompatibility between the responsibilities of members of the investment committee and their responsibilities as officers serving the government of Canada in other capacities. However, since that time the large deficit resulting from the actions of the government in the field of fiscal policy has shown there is now a real and important difference between the policies which ought to be followed with respect to the investments of the unemployment insurance fund and the course of action which the government believes it should follow in the management of the public debt. The heavy unemployment during the fiscal year 1958-59 caused a severe drain on the unemployment insurance fund, as is indicated by the figures in the reply given to the hon. member for Gloucester.
How much?

In 1957 the fund was $852 million in round figures, and on June 30, 1960, some $296 million. As I say, that figure of $296 million is not the last figure, if you take into account the actual losses I have mentioned and the book losses to which I will make reference later. Having in mind the necessity for maintaining the liquidity of this fund in the face of the unemployment problem, I believe these losses could and should have been avoided, particularly if the fund had been maintained in a more liquid state, something which I say was desirable having in mind the heavy drain on the fund itself. There can be no doubt, as subsequent events have revealed, of the necessity of maintaining the liquidity of the fund. Hence the trustees of the fund in 1958
Supply-Labour
should have sold government securities at every profitable opportunity in order to increase its cash holdings.
This means also that, to the extent that the fund decided to purchase government securities, it should have bought three-month treasury bills, short term government bonds or other securities maturing at an early date. However, during this period the aims sought by the government in the field of debt management were the very opposite of the financial requirements of the unemployment insurance fund itself. Indeed, we know that the government was trying to meet its huge cash requirements by selling as many bonds as possible to the public. The government also attempted, through the conversion loan, to lengthen the term of public holdings of its bonds. In other words the avowed purpose of the government was to reduce the liquidity position of the public, while the basic requirement of the unemployment insurance fund was to increase its liquidity as much as possible. There was therefore a sharp conflict of interest between the fund and the government.
The basis of my criticism is that the investment transactions of the fund were not, during that period, in my judgment conducted in the interests of the fund, but were determined exclusively by the requirements of the government, and as a result the fund lost $20 million. I am not alone in this view. I have before me a view expressed by Mr. A. H. Cameron in a speech he made on June 9, 1960 in the city of Kingston. I wish to quote his words. I regret I do not have the newspaper which reported him, but I can get it after I have finished. He said this:
In the first quarter of 1959, U.I.C. sold $129 millions, including $30 millions conversion 1972's, and $45 millions other longs, realizing large losses, until a government loan postponed further selling. The story is similar this year. This liquidation reflects U.I.C.'s prior aid to debt management. Facing a winter of obvious unemployment, (after a large early 1958 bond liquidation) U.I.C. converted all its Victory bonds, even its reputed $89 millions 1959 and 1960 maturities-buying no bills until October, 1958. These short Victories would have helped in meeting claims-without large losses.
Mr. Coyne later told a commons committee that U.I.C. could not have sold its $308 million Victories during the conversion-. .. "It was too large for the market to take. It would have ruined the market. .." One might ask, "What market?" since over 2,000 larger bond accounts could deal in Victories with only one dealer officially representing the Bank of Canada or Loan Committee. The only real market was in Bank of Canada. This implies the bank denied to U.I.C. the cash prices it offered the public, the banks and others.
The conflict of interest-U.I.C.'s needs versus debt management, (not apparent while the fund grew or government ran cash surpluses), was created by parliament placing bank and finance officials on the U.I.C. committee. Government widened the benefits in 1958 so that the fund entered 1959 with increased outgo, shorn of its more liquid Victories

Supply-Labour
by the loan. Had an independent trustee forced $300 millions in Victories on Bank of Canada for cash, he would have faced a reinvestment problem, but UI.C. had as much right as chartered banks of Canada's short paper-or even specially created government short paper. Had this happened, 1959's sales would have pressured the short market, not the long, for the converted Victories would have been in Bank of Canada.
Then he concludes as follows:
Subordinating U.I.C.'s liquidity needs to debt management, was of transient benefit, for many long term bonds soon were sold'-at a loss to U.I.C. Debt management problems during the loan would have been greater if U.I.C.'s interests had prevailed. Yet the U.I.C. committee would have been spurning the loan conceived in their other capacities. I pray that parliament will never again place public servants in such an impossible dilemma. The stopgap aid to debt management is not worth the result.
In view of the criticisms we levelled last session on this point, it seems to me that the government must take full responsibility for the actual loss of $20 million, as a consequence of the conversion loan and of the government's debt management policy. But this is not the whole situation. The par value of the bonds left in the fund was estimated recently at about $296 million. This compares with more than $900 million at the end of 1956 and, in view of the present unemployment outlook, represents a dangerously low level.
However, the real value of those bonds, if they had to be sold at present, is much lower than the amount of $296 million. The price of the conversion bonds held by the fund is comparatively low, and if those bonds had to be liquidated it is not likely that the proceeds would exceed $250 million. Who in this committee, in the face of the prognostications of unemployment, even assuming it does not rise to a level higher than the period through which we are now traversing, will deny that that is a very serious situation? With the amount of $250 million in the fund will we see the depletion of the fund. We should have from the Minister of Labour, and from the Minister of Finance if necessary, a statement as to what the government proposes to do before we finally pass these items. It could very well be that at the end of 1961 nothing will be left in the fund which on June 30, 1957, stood at over $852 million.
Is it the intention of the government to do nothing until the fund has been depleted? Will the government reimburse the $20 million lost by the fund as a result of the mismanagement of that fund? What steps does the government intend to take to replenish the fund? Although the minister denied, correcting himself the next day, that the fund had borrowed money from the government this year, the government did through the Minister of Finance loan to the fund some moneys
IMr. Martin (Essex East).]
in the months of April and May of this year. I think the general totals of those loans are not too far different from the total loss of the fund to which I have directed the committee's attention.
Now, Mr. Chairman, last night I indicated what	were the realized	losses of	the	fund,what	the realized losses	were for	the	fiscalyear	prior to this one,	and what	the	booklosses were a year ago.	This year	the	book
losses are something in the neighbourhood of $42 million as compared with a book loss in the previous fiscal year of some $60 million. So the market value of the fund now, less advances, is not much more than $260 million, and not the $296 million reported by the Minister of Labour on July 22, 1960.
In spite of the recent improvement in the bond market the fund at the end of June showed a book loss, as I said a moment ago, of $42 million. There are no securities now left in the fund which nature before 1968. That will be found by examining the unemployment insurance securities portfolio. Unless there is a further sharp improvement in the bond market, or unless the government makes a substantial contribution to restore the cash position of the fund, a serious loss on bond sales will be sustained next winter, when the seasonal drain on the fund begins.
Apart altogether from that, no one can deny that the fund is in a precarious state. We have the right on this estimate, in fact a duty, to ask the Minister of Labour for his comments, and to ask him to indicate what the government proposes to do to put the fund in such a state that if it is called upon to provide assistance to the unemployed in the next ensuing period, there will be no difficulty in doing so.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to have the opportunity of following the hon. member for Essex East, because I had intended to deal very largely with the subject he has just dealt with, and to do so completely on its merits and not, I hope, be led away by political considerations. But one never knows. Certainly the ex-minister had a fine time to himself, indulging in that delightful practice of wisdom after the event. I have seldom heard more wisdom after the event in such a short time, particularly with regard to securities.
Mr. Chairman, when I was in business I had some experience in the field of securities, so I can well realize how the hon. member was enjoying himself by indulging, with his uninhibited joy, in wisdom after the event. All I can say on that matter is that as much as I respect the hon. member and his judgment in many ways, I would not consider him a great authority on the matter of securities. I would much rather trust the experienced and

skilled men who actually deal in these securities. But there was never anyone who dealt with securities, however skilled and prudent he was, who could not afterwards be shown with a little after the event wisdom to have made what looked like a mistake, and we have had a classic example of that this afternoon.
Having said that, I must say 1 quite agree with the hon. member for Essex East when he says that this fund is in danger, and it is because of that fact that I want to speak about it this afternoon. I want to raise a question which I believe goes to the very root of unemployment insurance. I want to point out that perhaps, without anyone ever intending it, over these last years we have almost I will not say inevitably but unconsciously and unintentionally slipped into the situation where the fund has become less and less an insurance fund and more and more a general welfare fund. Indeed, perhaps it is not going too far to say that there is a widespread disposition to regard it more and more as a kind of universal Santa Claus.
Let me say here that I do not want anything I say to be interpreted as criticizing harshly the people who have taken benefits from the fund which strictly speaking were not intended, because I intend to make the point that this change in attitude "growed like Topsy". People began to extend it, and then it was extended a little more and a little more. I will not go into a lot of detail because I believe every hon. member here today can illustrate for himself the various leniencies, extensions and stretchings out of this fund which has made it serve purposes for which it was never intended.
Let me say quickly, lest I forget later, that the reason this has come about is not wholly because of claimants on the fund, but is also due to the attitude of employers who have found it convenient for various reasons to make a kind of informal broadening out of the purposes of the fund. Whatever the reason is, I feel one should face the fact that the situation is serious and calls for action.
Of course another of the secrets of the hon. member for Essex East in his speech this afternoon is that the fund has been depleted in the last couple of years because we had unemployment. I must say I am awfully grateful to him him for that, because otherwise one might not have known. Of course it has been depleted because of unemployment, and we recognize that it has been depleted to some extent because of government action, and we are all responsible for that.
I do not propose to go into detail, but I hope this afternoon, as far as my voice will reach-of course it will not reach as far as
Supply-Labour
Churchill's-to direct the attention of a few, or perhaps more than a few, to the fact that as I said a moment ago the fund has lost its character as an insurance fund. I am not going to attempt to apportion responsibility; what I am trying to do is create a feeling that something should be done, and that we should all share it. Money is being consumed for reasons which were never intended and, furthermore, this means that unemployment figures have been distorted and exaggerated, to what extent I am not going to attempt to estimate; but anyone who has thought about this will agree that it has led to the distortion of unemployment figures in a way which was never intended and in a way which has added a great deal to the difficulties of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission.
Imagine a situation such as this vis-a-vis the income tax department or the customs department. Unfortunately, with regard to insurance we have this situation, and I think it is best to understand what the situation is. When I and my neighbours on my street insure our houses we realize what we are doing; we are clubbing together so that if there is a fire, money is available to compensate the owner. We do not expect to get that money back. It is perfectly clear that when we contribute to such a fund we are not entitled to get our money back. Yet with regard to unemployment insurance there is this strong psychological feeling; "there is our money in that fund, and we are entitled to get it back". People who would not dream of expecting the return of money in other circumstances get a feeling that this is their money and that they are entitled to get it back. In the first place they overlook the fact that it is not their money; that in fact they have paid less than half of it, and more than half has been put up by the employers and the government.
While I am not prepared to say how much of that money goes out over and above what would go out if the fund were on a strictly insurance basis, the instances I have seen indicate a very substantial amount indeed. Some of the figures are staggering. And, as the hon. member for Essex East has pointed out, over the past three years there has been a depletion of some $600 million.
I want to say a word about the attitude of employers, because that is very important. The co-operation of employers is needed to enable this stretching out or broadening out process-I do not know exactly how to describe it-to be carried on. This does not happen in connection with income tax; employers give accurate figures there, but in connection with unemployment insurance, apparently prompted by a desire to be good

Supply-Labour
fellows and partly because in various ways it is very convenient to them to have the insurance fund come in and take over care of people who are rated as unemployed, they do assist, and assist in a way which is very surprising and which I do not think would happen if we could persuade them to look at this question in a realistic manner.
I believe that what has to be done-and I do not despair of it-is that people have to be given a new point of view toward this question. Of course I do not think people are going to become more conscientious tomorrow than they are today, and I have no doubt this will need to be accompanied by strict regulations. Nevertheless we cannot simply leave this up to the people in the unemployment insurance commission. Public opinion has to be behind this. As the hon. member for Essex East reminds us, this is not chicken feed that we are talking about; this is a very important matter.
I hope I have not appeared to be speaking in a pious tone, and I hope I have not given the impression that I regard myself as superior to other people. I do not, and I hope I have not given that impression. I wanted to bring up what I consider to be a serious situation and to suggest a rational solution. I imagine that those who were responsible for creating this fund years ago did not anticipate the development which has now arisen. They thought they were setting up an insurance fund and nothing else, and that is what it should have remained.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Essex East that this thing is bound to come to a head and that it needs serious consideration and action. As I said, it has grown like Topsy. It is clear there is going to be a heavy unnecessary drain unless we do something about it, but I am bold enough to believe that the people of this country, even if they slipped inadvertently into a false situation, when they are convinced of it they will face up to what has happened. I believe this has been done to some extent at any rate by inadvertence.
It is not inadvertence. It is bad management.
Oh, I am trying to be nonpolitical for just a few moments.
May I ask a question?

I shall be finished in a minute or so, and I will try to answer questions then.
I believe that if we pull ourselves together -and I mean all of us, because this fast and loose attitude has been very widespread- something may yet be done to remedy the

situation. I hope someone else may have something to say on this subject; I hope I am not the only one to say something which may be a little unpopular. I suppose the only sensible thing to do is to get back to the insurance basis, and I believe if this is properly put to the people of this country they will do it, because they are not without common sense.

May I ask a question? It was suggested by the intervention of the hon. member for Trinity. The hon. gentleman disparages the argument of responsibility for this situation. He is an experienced businessman, having been a distinguished trust officer. Will he deny that from 1957 on there was a conflict of interest that justifies the charge of mismanagement?
Yes, I would deny it. These were responsible people of character in charge of this fund-
No one suggested they were not people of good character.
I deny the conflict of interest entirely.

My remarks will be very brief. I have had occasion many times in this house to express my opinions concerning the status of the unemployment insurance fund. I referred to this situation when I spoke last night on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour.
The hon. gentleman who just resumed his seat has acknowledged that the fund is presently in danger, and I would say to him that it is not necessary to be an authority on securities in order to see that the fund is indeed in great danger. The hon. member went on to say that in its present condition this fund is less an insurance fund than a general welfare fund. When the unemployment insurance commission was created under a Liberal administration it was created to be an insurance fund, and it was maintained as such by the former administration.
No.

I hear an hon. member, greatly concerned, say "No, no". The unemployment insurance fund is a trust fund which has been established to protect the working class of this country, and it has been built up through the contributions of the workers, the employers and the general public.
The records show that the fund was in good condition under the previous administration. When the present government took office on June 30, 1957 there was left in the fund the sum of $852 million. As at June 30 this year the fund was down to $296 million.

We know that under the present conditions of unemployment, under the conditions which were admitted this morning by the minister, and in view of the forecast given us for the next eight or 10 months, we must acknowledge that notwithstanding the increase of 30 per cent in contributions which was introduced last year and which has been in effect since September 1, 1959, the unemployment insurance fund on this same date next year will contain only in the vicinity of $150 million. I am sure the minister will agree that this amount is not sufficient to take care of the situation. Before this estimate is passed the minister should tell us what are the plans of the government for replenishing the fund.
Before resuming my seat I want to express my concern about certain applications of the act and the regulations of the unemployment insurance commission. I know there have been abuses, and a fund of this kind is subject to them, but there rests on the officials of the department the difficult responsibility of stopping, preventing and correcting such abuses. Because the fund is in a difficult condition is no justification for certain employees having advantage taken of them.
I wish to refer briefly to the family employee. Case after case has been brought to my attention since last fall. These people were denied unemployment insurance benefits because they were employed by their fathers. In most cases the employer was in the lumber, trucking or some other business and employed two or three of his sons instead of hiring strangers as his employees. I do not see how the commission can justify a decision that would deprive those members of the family of the benefits to which they are entitled.
This has happened in New Brunswick and Quebec. When these members of the family made application for unemployment insurance they were told that if they wanted to receive benefits they should not stay at home with their father but should get out on their own or room and board with a neighbour. This situation cannot be permitted to continue. In most cases these were married men with families. They were employed by their fathers in employment that would qualify them for unemployment insurance. They should be entitled to receive it.

Mr. Chairman, I have often felt that my speeches were stolen by hon. members of the Liberal party in this chamber, but this was the first time I felt that an hon. member of the Conservative party had stolen in the main what I intended to say. I refer to the remarks made by the distinguished hon. member for Greenwood. I did not agree 100 per cent with what he
Supply-Labour
said about this fund, but I endorse the greater portion of his remarks.
When the fund was originally set up it was established on insurance principles. Proof of that can be found in the way the fund grew. At one time we had close to a billion dollars in the fund. Then the Liberal party found that it was too good a vote catcher to resist, and they let the political implications of the fund get the better of the insurance principles. Unfortunately when the present government took over it did as it has done in respect of so many things, and carried on and expanded the problems created by the Liberals. The situation has worsened since the Conservatives took office. As the hon. member said, the fund today represents no insurance principles at all but is a kind of mixed up welfare fund.
With increasing frequency we see in the newspapers and elsewhere evidence of the fact that the fund is not so much abused as chiselled. Many hon. members know this from cases brought to their attention. I do not know how you draw a distinction between an abuse and chiselling, but apparently that distinction exists in the mind of the public. As the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out, people who would never think of chiselling in any other way think the fund is fair game. The past and present governments must share the responsibility for this type of thinking among the public today.
I have received letters from constituents complaining that they have paid into the fund for the last 10 or 12 years and never drawn a cent out from it, and inquiring if they could not be paid a dividend of some kind. I believe that underlines what the hon. member said about there being no accurate concept in the public mind about the insurance principles of the fund. I have discussed this with various people. Certainly I have no offhand solution to offer the government today, but I believe an investigation of the situation should be made so the matter could be corrected in the future. I will, however, throw out one or two suggestions which I hope will be of some value.
I recommend that the government embark on a program to educate the Canadian public with respect to the meaning of the unemployment insurance fund. The government could point out that if somebody does not pay in there will 'be nothing to draw out, and that if you take out more than you put in someone will have to pay double or there will be nothing to take out.
I also urge the government to consider devising some kind of incentive. Again I cannot offer a detailed plan. Perhaps it could be

Supply-Labour
worked in conjunction with the old age pension, and a dividend given upon retirement to people who have paid in all their lives and never had occasion to draw out. This would be a means of driving home to the public the fact that the fund is not a barrel into which they can all reach. This is in conjunction with the program of public education to which I referred.
As long as there is a little chiselling here and a little there we will have difficulty. As the old Scottish saying goes, "Many a mickle makes a muckle". The day will come when the position of the legitimately unemployed will be made completely hopeless. If the fund has decreased by $200 million a year over the last three years there must be something wrong. Either unemployment is worse than the government has admitted or something else is wrong. There is only a little over $200 million in the fund right now, so at the rate of decrease over the last three years the government has only one year to learn what the trouble is and correct it. It behooves this government to take action rapidly if it does not want to face an extremely serious problem within the next year or so.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take only a few moments of the time of the committee, but in rising to speak on this item I should like to reiterate what the hon. member for Wetaskiwin has said with regard to the unemployment insurance fund as it affects farm labour. Last year the minister mentioned that he was setting up a committee to make a special study of unemployment insurance as it affected the seasonal unemployed with reference to the farming industry, fishing and pulp wood cutting. I should like to say that I was very pleased at that time, and I want to commend the minister for taking this action. It is another indication, of course, of how seriously our government is taking the problem of unemployment in Canada.
As a result of the recommendation to set up the committee I sent out a questionnaire to all reeves and councillors in my riding of Moose Mountain, some 200 in number, asking for their opinion on this matter. I might say for the information of the minister that I received a very good cross section of replies. Percentagewise about 75 per cent to 80 per cent of the people replying suggested they were in favour of the government taking some action along this line. In mentioning the fact that they were in favour of the application of unemployment insurance to farm labour they did not say whether it should be on an optional basis.

We have a peculiar situation in the farming industry in Saskatchewan. We have a number of large farms which are following the trend of the agrarian change which is taking place in this industry owing to automation. As a result, some farmers who may have only one son in the family, with the co-operation of automation, can carry on an economic unit; whereas on the other hand a farmer down the road with no sons in the family finds that in order to carry on an economic unit and follow the trend that has developed in the farm industry he has to have access to farm labour.
In looking at the labour market we find that the farmer's son, if he is not employed in farming, has to leave the province of Saskatchewan to find employment, because basically it has been an agricultural area, and owing to the lack of industrial development there compared with some other parts of Canada the young men have to leave. The result is there is a shortage of qualified farm labour. We would be doing ourselves a great service in Saskatchewan in particular if we could develop some type of unemployment insurance that would affect farm labour and help to maintain our population.
It is interesting to note that 30 years ago we had approximately a million people in Saskatchewan. As a result of automation developing in the industry our population slipped to 865,000 a few years ago. That trend has been reversed, and at the present time we have about 902,000 or 903,000 people in Saskatchewan. If we had maintained the normal population growth of other provinces over that same period we would have had today around 1,400,000 people, but that does not need any explanation from me. Hon. members realize what it means to a province like Saskatchewan, or any other part of the country, from an economic point of view; therefore I think we should take a serious look at this proposition to see whether something can be done to include the agricultural industry in unemployment insurance.

Will the committee allow me two minutes to answer the hon. member who has just spoken regarding agricultural employment? I know of the interest of many hon. members on all sides of the house in this subject, and I should like to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that an interdepartmental committee is studying the extension of coverage to agriculture. However, there is a decided dearth of statistical information of the kind needed to assist the committee in arriving at its conclusions. As a consequence it has been necessary for the committee to make a survey of certain types of farming in certain areas to obtain some estimate of

the likely costs. This sample has of necessity been small, but it does provide some guidance. The survey is going on now.
I should like to put on record the following departments which are represented on the committee: unemployment insurance commission, finance, agriculture, bureau of statistics, insurance and privy council.

A number of phases of unemployment insurance have already been raised on this item 173, and undoubtedly before it is passed additional phases will be brought to the attention of the committee. It is not my intention to speak on phases already raised or to prophesy what may yet be raised. My purpose in rising at this time is to draw the attention of the minister to either certain regulations or interpretations of regulations. I do so, Mr. Chairman, because I note that the hon. member for Cape Breton South has honoured us with his presence. The hon. member has not spoken during the discussion of the estimates, but he has made a great number of interjections, especially regarding certain views expressed on problems in his own riding of Cape Breton South and suggestions that from an employment point of view it could be called a depressed area. That seemed to upset the hon. member, although he has not made a speech on it yet. Will the minister consider either changing certain regulations or stating what are the interpretations of certain regulations as they apply and have applied to the present situation in Cape Breton and Cape Breton South, because I believe, sir, Glace Bay comes within the constituency of the hon. member.

If the hon. member does not mind I should like to make an observation. When the hon. member for Essex East was speaking he said nothing about Glace Bay, New Waterford, or the surrounding towns. He emphatically said the city of Sydney, Nova Scotia. If he would just look at a recent statement by the mayor of Sydney he would see that it is in sharp contrast with what he said.
I take it now, sir, that the hon. member takes it that no reference was made to his own constituency?

No, you do not understand what was said at all. He referred specifically to the city of Sydney. I do not for a moment deny there are depressed sections in that area; I am speaking specifically of the city of Sydney. The mayor of Sydney recently referred to the prosperity of that city, and it does that city no good to have somebody who does not understand the situation there go about preaching that it is a depressed city, and by so doing discouraging any new industry or any new business which might wish
Supply-Labour
to come into that city. This is only another approach that is detrimental to that city, the Liberal approach in the maritimes.
I now understand the confusion of the hon. member.
You are referring to the hon. member for Essex East.
I am sorry; I have the floor, if you do not mind.
Yes, but speak factually.

My hon. friend is confused in that he did not recognize, as I think most of us did, that the hon. member for Essex East was referring to the report of the employment office in Sydney, which covers the entire area, including the hon. member's constituency.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
As soon as I sit down, yes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: The member for Essex East said the city of Sydney.
The city of Sydney is the regional office for the entire area, including the constituency of the hon. member who has just spoken.
On a point of order-
I said I would be very happy to-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I am sorry; I beieve I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is rising on a point of order.

My point is this; that the hon. member now speaking is interpreting the views of the hon. member for Essex East, and not only was the hon. member for Cape Breton South confused but this whole committee was confused with what he had to say about the unemployment situation in Moncton when he claimed that there were so many thousand unemployed.
That is not a point of order.
The hon. member does not know the difference anyhow.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
According to the rules, if the hon. member has an objection to any statement he may rise after the hon. member who has the floor has completed his remarks and make his correction.

Supply-Labour
May I say that the hon. member is certainly confused now, because he is referring to Moncton and I am speaking about his own constituency.
But he was talking about Moncton.

I would be very happy if the hon. member would make a speech instead of interjecting so often. As a matter of fact I wonder why he is here, because he only interjects and does not make speeches. I said I was very happy that the hon. member had honoured us with his presence, because I should like to ask the views of the Minister of Labour in connection with certain regulations as they exist, and certain interpretations made thereof, with relation to representations that have been made by the united mine workers of America at Glace Bay, in the hon. member's constituency. The best way for me to introduce this matter is to read directly the information that comes to our hands. I have here, sir, a telegram received by us this month which states as follows:
Local 4520 UMWA in session tonight respectfully request that present UIC regulations be amended to conform with the basic understanding governing payment of benefits. Some 450 coal miners employed in No. 4 colliery Dominion Coal Company Limited in Glace Bay are completely without income for a period of two weeks due to cut-backs in the Nova Scotia coal industry and regulations that prohibit payment of UIC benefits. Respectfully request use of your good office to have this extreme injustice eliminated.
We in this group, sir, to the best of our ability try to help people in all constituencies. This matter was taken up, therefore, with the unemployment insurance commission, and the reply we received was:
Section 152 of the regulations provides that the waiting period may be waived if
(a)	a new period of entitlement immediately follows the end of a previous period of entitlement, and
(b)	the claimant's aggregate earnings in the last two weeks of the old period of entitlement are not more than one week's benefit plus allowable earnings.
The situation with regard to the 400 miners is that they were laid off during the week commencing 12 June and their periods of entitlement ended on 18 June. Their new entitlement started on 19 June, but they cannot meet the conditions in (b) above because their earnings in the weeks commencing 5 June (when they worked) and 12 June were too high to permit of the waiver.
I am advised that the miners received payment of unemployment insurance benefits for the week commencing 12 June but as previously stated the week commencing 18 June was the week in which they were required to serve their waiting period and therefore they received no benefit payment for this period.
Yours sincerely,
Laval Fortier Chief Commissioner
Now, sir, in view of the telegram I have read, in view of the answer received from
[The Chairman.]
the chief commissioner, may I ask on behalf of the united mine workers, local 4520, at Glace Bay, in the constituency of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, whether this interpretation of the regulations was wrong or whether the regulations could possibly be amended, especially in view of the fact that the unemployed workers at Glace Bay say this is an extreme injustice which they would like to have eliminated.

This matter was first brought to my attention by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who at that time was in the offices of the local union and who made available to me the information to which the hon. member refers. I was then in communication with the president of the union on the long distance telephone. I immediately brought it to the attention of the unemployment insurance commission, and the interpretation of that regulation is correct.
This has been brought to the attention of the union, pointing out that under this regula-ion the miners were not entitled to benefits. The only thing that can be done is to either have the regulation amended or to submit this regulation to the unemployment insurance advisory committee, the membership of which is composed of representatives of labour and management on an equal basis.
May I ask the minister if he has referred the request of the united mine workers in Glace Bay to the advisory committee?

No, Mr. Chairman, because the regulation is there. If consideration is given to obtaining the advice of that committee on whether this regulation should be in existence, then that consideration can be given and the regulation submitted for their advice.

Do I understand, then, that the minister does not feel he has a responsibility when matters of this nature are brought to his attention by any member of this house, and that he should refer them to the advisory committee, asking their advice?

This regulation has been in existence for some time and has applied in many instances of the same nature. Now, if it is felt by the commission that this regulation is unfair then the commission, in consultation with me, may agree that consideration be given to submitting this regulation to the advisory committee.
Does the minister not agree that if he receives a complaint of this nature, and he says he received it from the hon. member himself, he should refer it to the advisory committee?

We receive complaints from all over Canada about every regulation that is applied by the unemployment insurance commission. Surely the hon. member would not suggest that on the basis of the complaints we have received about every regulation in the Unemployment Insurance Act we should submit every one of them to the advisory committee?
Not on an individual basis, but if it comes from a responsible trade union or if it comes from a member of this house, yes.
We have had representations on almost every regulation from time to time over the years from responsible groups of people and representatives of the workers.

I am in danger of being accused of filibustering if I speak, because the opposition seems to take that attitude toward any backbencher on the government side who speaks. I should like to say this, sir, to the hon. member for Vancouver East. When this question arose I, along with the president and secretary treasurer of the local affected, not 4520 but 4530, my own local in Glace Bay, in conjunction with the officers of the united mine workers, followed through with every possible step to alleviate this hardship.
On what date?

I do not remember the date, but it was the date on which the matter arose. I was present in the offices of the united mine workers and I communicated with the Minister of Labour in Ottawa, the minister of labour in Nova Scotia, and made efforts to communicate with the premier of Nova Scotia because this regulation was causing hardship among the members. The Caledonia local, 4530, has thanked me along with the president and secretary treasurer, for the efforts we made in this connection.
As to the regulations, they are well aware of the fact that the unemployment insurance advisory commission has labour representation in order to look after the interests of labour. They realize that this is an insurance to us. We then attempted to get the unemployment insurance assistance benefits, and we made every effort in this regard to help the miners over this rough period they were obliged to go through because broken time in the mines at that particular period, affected their unemployment insurance for that coming week. What brought about the three week period without any remuneration was the fact that the set-up in the mines is such that when you work a week, you do not get paid for that particular week you work but the following week. That is what contributed to the hardships down there, namely the
Supply-Labour
fact that they were obliged to wait three weeks in order to draw their salaries from the company.
That is a long wait.

Certainly it is a long wait. I appreciate that fact. I may tell the hon. member for Vancouver East that I am well aware of everything that has affected the miners in that area. I do not need the hon. member for Essex East or the hon. member for Vancouver East or any other member of the committee to point out to me the difficulties through which the miners have been going, not since 1957 but back to 1945 and further, when the previous administration was in power. Let me tell you that the present conditions prevailed under a Liberal administration. In the province of Nova Scotia 23 coal mines closed down in the period from 1946 to 1956.
How many closed down in the last three years? How many are closing down now?

None of the big operations have closed down in the last three years. They are facing it, but we are doing everything possible to avoid it. I will tell you now that 23 coal mines closed down in that period between 1946 and 1956, and none of the larger operations have closed down since this government came into office. Some smaller operations have closed down, but there are also a few small operations which have opened up with the assistance of the Nova Scotia government.
In order to remind the hon. member of what is going on, may I say that the telegram he received was from the president of local 4520, the brother of the only remaining C.C.F. member in Nova Scotia. As to the area about which he is concerned, I might remind him that regardless of the situation in Nova Scotia as it is today, the miners' union, the steel workers and the workers of Cape Breton have put their trust in the Prime Minister and Bob Stanfield, and rightly so.

To get away from the political implications for a moment, may I turn to something else. The minister mentioned that one possible solution for this particular problem that has been raised has to do with amendments to the existing legislation. From what he said I gather that either the amendments or recommendations for them would come from the advisory committee. But he also said that before they could recommend any changes, complaints would have to be forwarded to them by the minister or the commission. My question is this. How can the advisory committee realize

Supply-Labour
that there are any complaints and that there is any need for amendment of the existing legislation if the great number of the complaints mentioned by the minister never get past his office?

I will say this, Mr. Chairman. I will submit this regulation, or ask the commission to consider this regulation; and if in their opinion they feel that it should be considered by the advisory committee, then they will forward it on to the advisory committee.
What is the make-up of this advisory committee? Who are on the committee? How are they appointed, and how long do they hold office?

There are four employer representatives and four employee representatives. On the employee side there are two representatives from the Canadian Labour Congress, one representative from the Canadian and Catholic Federation of Labour, and one representative from the brotherhood of railway employees. On the employer side there is a representative from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, a representative from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, a representative from the Canadian Construction Association and one representative from the Canadian Railway Association.
Do the committees meet of their own volition, or do they meet only when something is referred to them? In other words have they the power of initiating recommendations to the labour department?
Under the act they are empowered to report the state of the unemployment insurance fund, and to meet when the commission submits for their recommendation a certain regulation.

In other words the advisory committee can meet only on a direction of the commission, and can deal only with matters which are referred to it by the minister or through the unemployment insurance commission. Is that correct?
It is an advisory committee to the commission.
It can meet only when something is referred to it. It cannot meet of its own volition or bring in its own recommendations?
That is right.
Do you think that is a democratic procedure?
That is the way the committee is set up under the act.
As to persons who are possibly entitled to draw unemployment insurance for some months but who become university students, can they continue to draw unemployment insurance?
Each case is considered on its own merits.
In some cases it can be done.
In some cases?
Yes, having regard to the availability of the student for work. That is the basis on which he can draw unemployment insurance.

May I ask for a further point of information on something I have never been able to get quite clear from reading the act. To my knowledge there are a great many persons who have been previously employed but who want to try, when they are unemployed, to get out on their own and earn their living. I know a great number of such persons in my constituency. They may be electricians, carpenters or painters. If they endeavour to help themselves in this way and they hit a bad period, as they do, in order to be covered when they are endeavouring to do this are they entitled to contribute to unemployment insurance?

If they go into business for themselves and, during the period of the first two years, become unemployed, they may apply for unemployment insurance benefits because of the fact that it is within the two-year period only that a person can claim benefits. Then if it is found that they are genuinely unemployed in that respect they would be eligible for unemployment insurance.

How do they contribute in this period? I am greatly interested in this matter. When you have these people who want to try to get out and help themselves, and who are doing so, is there any way in which, during that temporary period of a year or two years when they are trying to help themselves, they can pay in to unemployment insurance?
No; no self-employed person can be insured.
In other words they are not eligible at all?
No.
Item agreed to.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROVISION OF CANADIAN SIGNALS PERSONNEL AND EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has already been informed that the government has been giving consideration, in consultation with the secretary general, to the United Nations inquiry as to whether Canada would be in a position to provide signals personnel and equipment as part or in support of the United Nations force in performing their important role in the Congo. These consultations were necessary in order to ascertain in detail the requirements of the force commander and to relate them to facilities and personnel available in Canada.
I am now in a position to say that the government has decided to provide, subject to parliamentary approval of a resolution which will be placed on the order paper today, certain military forces, including equipment, for the following signals units: a signals detachment at United Nations headquarters in Leopoldville which will include a signals office, a message centre, 100-line switchboard and linemen and dispatch riders; five ground to air communication links; twelve mobile wireless detachments; eight cipher detachments, and a small headquarters for the command and administration of Canadian troops in the Congo. Preparatory action has been taken to provide for the formation of such new units within the services as may be required, the selection and immunization of soldiers, the concentration of troops and their equipment, and the movement of them by the most expeditious means, again subject to parliamentary approval of a resolution to that effect.
Since additional information is required on the tasks which the Canadian contingent will be asked to perform and on the conditions under which these tasks will be carried out, a reconnaissance party of six officers is being
dispatched to the Congo immediately. It is due to leave Montreal this evening and to arrive in Leopoldville on August 1. In the meantime, awaiting parliamentary consideration, the members of the Canadian signals contingent are being selected and immunized against tropical diseases. Then immediate concentration within Canada will be provided for, and as I said a moment ago those chosen will be sent as soon as they are ready and transport becomes available.
The resolution in question will be placed on the order paper, as I say, and it will ask approval for participation of Canadian forces in the United Nations operations in the Congo. I think that is a step in keeping with traditional practice, and it is particularly important at this time that there be full recognition and acceptance by parliament of this step in the preparation and maintenance of a United Nations force. No more important or significant step has been taken in recent years than the one now being taken by the United Nations in the Congo, and the cooperation of those nations which it is believed are the most appropriate to make a contribution renders desirable full co-operation and anticipation of parliamentary approval.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROVISION OF CANADIAN SIGNALS PERSONNEL AND EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister may be assured that in observing the traditions established in this house, certainly since the end of the first world war, that a project of this kind should be preceded by a resolution, he will find that such a resolution will be given strong support by the membership of this house. We recognize that in the turbulent days in which we live, the best way of maintaining order is by giving to the collective strength of the nations of the world, through the United Nations, the opportunity of making a contribution in the preservation of that order.
The Prime Minister has not indicated if Canada has been asked to supply more than the kind of forces he has outlined. To the extent, therefore, that we have been asked for these particular signals forces there will be general accord. The secretary general of the United Nations has stated that he envisages that this particular project of the United Nations in the Congo will not be of short duration, and that it may last for a period of as long as five years. In that event, it is to be anticipated that Canada will be asked

Inquiries of the Ministry to contribute more than specialized military forces, referred to in the statement of the Prime Minister.
I agree fully with what the Prime Minister has said, that this effort of the United Nations in which Canada will share to this limited extent at this time, represents the growing strength of the United Nations as an instrument for the preservation of peace. We have the precedent of the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East, an organism with which Canada has had so much to do. That precedent, backed up by the United Nations observation group in Lebanon and the presence of the United Nations in Jordan, is a precedent which has made possible the intervention of the United Nations in the Congo. Whether the United Nations military forces now in the Congo are para-military only, in the sense that the United Nations force in the Middle East is, or whether it is to be given greater power, is not yet clear. In any event, the Prime Minister may be assured that when this resolution comes before the house, it will receive the responsible consideration which its great objectives deserve.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROVISION OF CANADIAN SIGNALS PERSONNEL AND EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
The
members of this group endorse most heartily the announcement made by the Prime Minister concerning this contribution to the maintenance of peace in a troubled portion of the world. As a matter of fact we are delighted with this step being taken by the government, perhaps as a first step toward an even greater effort on the part of Canada in this direction.
We believe that Canada can best play an active role in the maintenance of peace by being ready on all occasions to supply to the limit of her capacity forces required by the United Nations in causes such as this.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Following the recent opening of the 12 million bushel grain elevator at Baie Comeau, Quebec, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, can the minister outline what effect this new elevator capacity will have on the handling of this year's grain movement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BAIE COMEAU, QUE.-EFFECT OF OPENING OF NEW ELEVATOR
speechtext:
This is a very important development indeed, and I think congratulations are due to the Cargill Grain Company Limited of Winnipeg for their enterprise in having this elevator erected and in operation so early. It is only about a year and a half since they started their building operations. The fact is that this elevator will provide extra storage for Canadian grain and will add at least 7 million bushels of storage capacity. During the course of next winter we shall see what effect it has on the shipment of Canadian grain. It is expected that they will be able to ship the year around, and this will be of advantage.
It is important to note that United States grain may use this particular elevator, as has been the custom with other elevators on the eastern seaboard and in the St. Lawrence region. The arrangements made by the board of grain commissioners with the Cargill company are to the effect that 60 per cent of the storage capacity of this elevator shall be available for Canadian grain.

What was being discussed was the question raised by the Leader of the Opposition as to whether the Minister of Labour was prepared to give to this committee a comprehensive appreciation of the prospects for employment over the next few months and the coming winter. In the course of that discussion the minister told my hon. friend from Essex East that he considered it was too early to make any such forecast. I believe that was the position taken by the minister, that at the beginning of August it was too early to make any forecast as to what the employment situation is likely to be. We realize that forecasts are only forecasts, but what is the position likely to be in the coming winter?
I stated, and I want to repeat it, sir, that I believe such a forecast already exists, unless the minister or the Prime Minister or someone on their behalf has told this branch of the minister's department not to make it. We know from past experience when we were in office that forecasts of this character were made, and were certainly made this early in the year. We know also that the government is very anxious to keep secret now what the Prime Minister was not so anxious to keep secret when he could get a cheap political advantage out of it two years ago. We know from the refusal of the Minister of Trade and Commerce this morning that the forecast made in his department is not available to the house or to the Canadian people, though there can be no doubt it exists unless that one, too, has been cut out by this government because it is afraid to have such forecasts made.
The plain fact is that this government has done everything in its power, throughout the whole of the year 1960, to stop any flow of information to the Canadian people about economic and employment prospects for the coming year, except the optimistic statements made by the Minister of Labour last February and those made by the Prime Minister in March on television, which apparently were backed up by nothing beyond their reading of the stars. At least we have not been told what they were backed up by.
Then the minister, in order to reinforce his position, to reinforce this new constitutional position, this new respect for parliament, this new consideration for the rights of people, said last night when he was being pressed:
Mr. Chairman, I am a member of a government that was elected with an overwhelming majority

by the people of this country and I will perform my duties to the best of my ability.
In other words, this minister apparently does not consider it necessary to have any advice. He has the backing, or he said he had two years ago, of the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people, so he can do what he pleases without consulting anyone, without telling the House of Commons what he is proposing to do, without taking the people into his confidence. In other words, "We have a majority, so whatever we like to do we do not need to bother explaining to you". This is the new doctrine of the Conservative party. It is not really a new doctrine, because it sounds very much like-
An old Liberal one.

I suggest that the hon. gentleman go a little farther back into history. This is exactly the same attitude that was taken by Mr. Bennett when he was prime minister between 1930 and 1935. It is a typical Tory attitude. I challenge any hon. member to show, in the whole of the period when Hon. Milton Gregg was minister of labour in this country, that he ever took any such attitude or ever refused to give parliament any information that was available in his department.
Would the hon. member say I was wrong if I told him I have a strong recollection of Mr. St. Laurent taking exactly that position on a certain occasion?

That is not the
position taken by this government with regard to the economic survey.

The hon. member for
Greenwood asked me a question which I think was really a declaration, but I take no exception whatever to his declaration. His recollection was that he remembered some occasion when Mr. St. Laurent had taken a similar position. I do not happen to recall it, but I should not like to quarrel with the hon. gentleman. However, I should like to see the particulars. There are, of course, many communications that come to the Department of External Affairs and to the other departments of government which every government might properly keep confidential. But surely the estimate of the prospects of employment does not fall into this category; or if it does, what are they afraid of? If it does, what is it that concerns them?
This is something that it is hard indeed for me to answer. I admit that a forecast made by a civil servant for the guidance of ministers, such as the "Economic Outlook for 1957" which was tabled in this house by the Prime Minister on January 20, 1958 or a document of that sort should not be made

public. I make that admission at once. What was that document for? That document was not for any other purpose than to assist ministers in working out policies; and to ensure that ministers would get the utmost frankness in the advice that was given to them and to protect the validity of the forecasts themselves it is necessary to protect the anonymous public servants who prepared such forecasts. It seems to me that is a reasonable position to take, particularly in the whole economic realm where such forecasts could easily have the effect, if they were published prematurely, of influencing the economic climate in a way that might be adverse to the national interest.
If the Minister of Labour is irguing that to give a forecast of employment for next winter is going to influence the level of employment next winter, I wish he would make that argument. If he wants to make that argument I am sure that we would listen to it with great interest and would consider carefully what there was in it. As for myself, at first blush I do not see how it could have any such effect. However, if the minister feels that it is in the national interest to conceal any official forecast of this kind or to hide it, in the light of the speech made by the Prime Minister on January 20, 1958-* which speech presumably set the tone for the present government-I think the minister would need to do a great deal of explaining in order to clarify that situation.
But if he has no such explanation, and if the only reason he is hiding this forecast is that it is a gloomy report, as I suspect is unhappily the case, may I say this. If the only reason he is hiding it is that he knows this government has no policy, has no measures by means of which to cope with this situation, then I say he is derelict in his duty to the Canadian people and is not showing for parliament the regard that this government promised the people of Canada it would have when it obtained its mandate two years ago.

Mr. Chairman, the same questions were asked yesterday. I have nothing further to add to what I said yesterday in respect of these matters.

This is a strangely negative attitude for a minister to take to our efforts to get information as to what the employment situation or the unemployment situation is likely to be in the coming winter and what the government is planning to do about it. We are now approaching August.

The winter period will be on us before long. We have been told that there are 43 economists in this branch of the Department of Labour whose job presumably-and I am sure they are highly qualified-is to give the minister advice on the economic outlook and particularly on the employment outlook. Yet the minister tells us that notwithstanding these 43 economists and the advice which they no doubt are giving him and the work in which they are no doubt engaged, it is too early to make any forecast, based on that advice, as to what the situation is likely to be in the autumn and winter. Surely that is a terrible reflection on the lack of planning in the government at the present time in respect of this vital problem of employment.
We were told last night that there is a cabinet committee under the chairmanship of the Associate Minister of National Defence working on this problem. Surely they must have before them some information on which they can make their reports, some information perhaps produced for them by, among other sources, these 43 economists that we are now talking about. What kind of situation is this cabinet committee planning to meet this winter? What kind of situation are the minister and his department planning to meet? All the minister told us last night was that it was going to be extremely difficult to figure out what kind of situation he will be obliged to meet. We are in August or are about to be in August, and all we learn about the situation that may confront us this winter is that it is going to be extremely difficult to find out what that situation is going to be.
That is a shocking basis, Mr. Chairman, for any kind of planning to meet the situation. With great respect I suggest to the minister that he owes it to this committee to tell us more than he has told us. As a matter of fact he has told us nothing.
