minister whether, since the discussion last night, he has had an opportunity, or has taken the opportunity, to discuss with the director of this economic research division or any of its personnel the questions put to him by hon. members last night. The minister has finally acknowledged that there was a confidential report made to him; and now having ascertained that fact may we ask, will the minister tell us whether or not, as a result of efforts made between eleven o'clock last night and eleven o'clock this morning, he has been able to get information which this committee requires, before we can properly pass this particular estimate?

Mr. Chairman, yesterday I said that any forecasts for the coming winter months could not be made until some time toward the end of August. This is true, and no report has been given me because of that circumstance.
If the minister has been given no report by his officials on this matter, something which is hard to credit.

I endeavour to read all the reports which are available in order to assess in my own mind what the situation may be, but based on the experience in the past two winters, and based on the present situation it is evident that this government views the situation as serious, because of the measures that are being taken and other measures that are to be taken to deal with it.

If the reports from the minister's own economic division on the situation which may confront us this winter in terms of unemployment are not available until the end of August, then on the basis of what information is the cabinet committee on unemployment, headed by the Associate Minister of National Defence, operating? Where does that committee get its basis of information?
Hon. members of the opposition have given us the basis of the information. They say there are reports available, a Bank of Canada report and other reports.

Just before the Leader of the Opposition spoke the minister made an admission that we have been asking him to make for some hours. He said-and he will correct me if I interpret him wrongly -that the government, after examining the reports which have been made, regards the situation in the immediate future as serious.
Based on past experience we say that unemployment is a serious situation, and as long as unemployment exists it is always a serious situation.

We are not talking about what is in existence. We are talking about what the situation is likely to be in the immediate future. I understood the minister to say that the government regards the situation in the ensuing period as serious. If that is a correct statement, and I understood the minister to say that, I regard it as an advance on the position the minister has taken thus far in this debate.

I can correct that right away. I said that based on our experience in the past two or three winters and on the present situation as it exists at the moment, this government regards unemployment as a serious situation and has taken the lead in a number of projects, and others will be undertaken in the future.

Supply-Labour

Quite. As I say, that statement, confirmed by the minister, advances us considerably.
The minister said in reply to a question put by the Leader of the Opposition that he would not have any estimate until the end of August. I ask him the following question. Is it not a fact that his predecessor was supplied with a report for the summer period? Is it not a fact that his predecessor was supplied with a report prepared in the month of May, forecasting the employment situation in the summer period? If that is a fact, and I assert it to be a fact, has the minister discontinued that practice? If he has not discontinued the making of such a quarterly report, will he then explain to the committee how it is he cannot give us any estimate on the situation during the summer until the summer is over, namely, as he said, until the end of August?
No practice has been discontinued, as I said yesterday in the debate. I must remind the hon. member that these reports are confidential.

The minister keeps saying that they are confidential, and he would not make a confidential report available. But as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, this government did not regard confidential documents as being confidential and as not capable of being produced in this chamber. That is the position.
After they are outdated.

The hon. member says "After they are outdated". All he and his friends have to do is read the remarks made by the Prime Minister in 1958 and note what he had to say about a confidential document which he used to his advantage at that time but which, since that time, this government has refused to give to the house.
We are not asking for confidential documents to be produced. We are saying that this government has created a precedent for itself, and it would not be difficult on this account for the government to make such documents available. But since the government takes the position it does, we are asking that the Minister of Labour, at a time when we are discussing if we should pass these estimates, should simply tell us in general terms what recommendations and what assessments are made by the officials with regard to the future so that we in this parliament may determine if the provisions the government has in mind are adequate. We are not asking for something which is unreasonable. This persistent refusal on the part of the Minister of Labour to give us this information can only result in one conclusion, and

that is that this government has no policy whatsoever to meet unemployment.
Oh.

Hon. members say "oh". Let them deny that there is anything lacking in the logic of my conclusion. The hon. member who is interjecting now is a respected and responsible member, and I am sure he cannot deny the logic of what I am saying. Either I am right or parliament as we understand it does not exist in this country.
Nonsense.

An hon. member says "nonsense". I understand parliament to be a place where the elected representatives of the people have the right to ask from those entrusted with the responsibility of government information which will justify voting of moneys asked for by Her Majesty's government. That is the constitutional position. We have had from the Minister of Labour in response to our request a refusal to give information which it is an inherent right of this parliament to receive, and if the minister persists in refusing to give this information then it is our responsibility to determine whether we shall let these estimates pass. That is our responsibility, and it is a grave decision to make, but it is a decision we have to make if our democratic practices mean anything.
Does that mean you are going to ask for a cut in them?

The hon. member who comes from a labour constituency, should be the first to rise and support what I am saying. The hon. member comes from what is a depressed area, notwithstanding his denial of that fact last night. The hon. member comes from a constituency where last winter thousands of men were out of work; over 6,000, as my hon. friend reminds me. I come from a constituency where there are now between
6,000	and 8,000 unemployed, and it is because of this that I feel I have a duty in this committee to elicit from the Minister of Labour whatever information he can give us in order to determine what can be done in this country to meet this problem. Surely that is not unfair. Surely that is not asking the government or the minister anything that is improper. If the Minister of Labour says this situation is an extremely complicated one, and the government cannot be expected to have all the solutions to this problem-
You never did.
The hon. member says that we never did. Well, we never had the problem.
Well, I know all about the problem, and from 1935 to 1939 the boys were walking the streets-

Yes, the hon.
member is right; from 1930 to 1935 thousands of people did walk the streets-
He said 1939.
What I am saying is this-
Take your time.

Hon. gentlemen may make it difficult for this discussion to continue if they wish. They may cause delay but it will not make any difference, because we propose to discuss these estimates until we feel we have discharged our responsibility. There is no doubt about that. We can stay here for a long time.
So can we.
Apparently that is what we are going to do, because we are going to get answers to these questions or we are going to know why.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Don't be so pompous.

I ask the Minister of Labour if he will tell us that the problem is such that it is unfair to expect the government to provide solutions. Then that becomes a matter for argument. But that is not what the minister says. The minister just refuses to make any statement. He refuses to make any declaration other than the fact that this is a confidential report.
I ask the minister to reconsider that answer in the light of this discussion. If the minister will give us a statement based on what he believes are the realities; if he excuses the administration from responsibility and gives valid arguments for this, there can be no criticism of that position, other than to point out, if that is the situation, that he government will not be regarded as having realized its assurances to the Canadian people. But the simple issue now is whether or not parliament is entitled to receive this basic information.

Mr. Chairman, it is obvious from the discussion which took place last night in the hour and a half before we adjourned at eleven o'clock, and from what has been said thus far in our sitting today, that it is not the intention of the Minister of Labour to file any reports or information he has received, because as he has reiterated time after time they are confidential documents. In view of that fact we cannot help but wonder if he could not make that information available by following the
Supply-Labour
precedent established by the Prime Minister in tearing off the front page of the document. It was on that basis that we got the information before, so how about tearing off the front page again?
I should like to ask the hon. member a question, Mr. Chairman. Can the hon. member prove that?
You will find it in Hansard.
You will find many false statements in Hansard.
You will find there was no front page.
And who tore it off?
We do not know who tore it off.
You said it was the Prime Minister.
It must have been some member of the government, because no hon. member of the opposition could have torn it off.
How could you know? How do you know what transpired in the six months of its existence prior to its being brought into this chamber? How do you know whether the cover was on or off?
I do not know about that. I only know that when it was brought in the cover had been removed, and if it was a good precedent then it is good now.

Mr,
Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I suggest that what is happening at this moment indicates that we are discussing matters which are quite irrelevant to the estimates of the Department of Labour. This has been obvious, I think, for some little time in the light of the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East. We can see now where this type of discussion is leading. It is a discussion of something that happened in another parliament in connection with the Prime Minister and a report issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This has no bearing whatever on the item that is now before us concerning the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour. I most respectfully suggest that all this discussion is completely irrelevant, and that hon. members should turn their attention to discussion of the item before us.

Mr. Chairman, I hope you will not accept this invitation of the minister to close off this discussion of the economic situation in this country and our desire to

Supply-Labour
get information from the department most concerned about that situation, the Department of Labour.
Even if you seek to get it by means of irrelevant discussion.
I do not think I am irrelevant, but if 1 am let me say that I would rather be irrelevant than irresponsible.
The hon. member succeeds in being both.

The item we are now discussing relates to the economics and research branch. That has to do with all matters relevant to labour and therefore all matters relevant to employment and unemployment. If discussions in previous parliaments under the present government and the present Prime Minister have established that this question of advice to the government could be discussed, it is just as relevant today as it was then. Because of the irresponsibility of the government it seeks to use these things for its own political expediency, denying information to parliament except when the government wants parliament to have the information. If there is any irrelevancy and irresponsibility it has been demonstrated on the other side.
Apparently today we are to be denied that information, with the cover on or off. That being the case, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour if he will comment with respect to a statement made at the end of April by such outstanding men as Mr. David Mansur, real estate consultant, Mr. W. H. Evans, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and Mr. James Coyne of the Bank of Canada as reported in the Star. On the basis of a survey taken, these three men have said that next fall will witness a turndown in the economy, and next winter will see unemployment worse than last year and indeed it will equal the postwar peak of unemployment.
These men are all good Canadians. I mention that because the minister told us last evening on three occasions that he was a good Canadian. I do not doubt that for a moment. In fact I do not doubt that all hon. members of this committee are good Canadians who look forward to a great future for Canada.
In view of the statement made by these good Canadians will the minister tell us if he agrees with their analysis? If he does not, how and why does he disagree? If there is any agreement at all, what in the view of the minister will be done to meet the situation? What is being done about it now?

Mr. Chairman, I can only reiterate what I said in response to the same question earlier. It is quite evident that the government are concerned about the situation. We have expanded our effort, are contributing to the training of unemployed workers on a higher scale of cost to the federal government, and the Prime Minister has said that other projects are under consideration. One has to have respect for the opinions of these people but based on our own experience in the past two winters and based on the present situation as indicated by the studies of the dominion bureau of statistics, it is surely quite evident that the government is taking steps to see that the situation does not worsen in the coming months.

I think everyone here will commend the government for all the steps that have been announced. There is no question of that. But I should like to put this question to the minister. He quoted three times last night a statement of the Prime Minister-I forget the exact wording-that new consideration is being given to the matter and at the appropriate time other policies may be announced. In view of the fact that we are now very close to August, will the minister inform us why, on the basis of information they must have within the department, within the government and outside, it is the policy to withhold announcements until parliament is no longer sitting. I expect we shall not be sitting more than another week-
Hear, hear.

I gather some hon. members want to go home. I do, too. I have been home only six days this year. I would like to get home, but I am staying here until this house has concluded its business and prorogued, because that is the job for which I was elected.
So are we.

Quite a number have left already. In view of the present serious situation, and what looks like a worsening one, why are announcements not made by the government while parliament is in session and can deal with government policy?

Mr. Chairman, with respect to those matters on which decisions have been arrived at, the decisions have been announced in this House of Commons. I refer to such matters as housing, municipal winter works programs, training for unemployed workers, home improvement loans and so forth. With respect to all those things and which decisions have been arrived at, announcements have

been made. There are other matters with respect to which decisions have not yet been arrived at, and we are doing everything possible to expedite them as much as we can.

How are they going to be financed; by treasury board order? Because you will not have the authority of the estimates. We would like the minister to have authority for whatever is required to take care of the situation.
I am not the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, surely we had the right to expect, when the minister's estimates are brought before the house in the closing days, we hope, of the session, that the minister would give us a comprehensive analysis of the economic and employment situation in this country, and a comprehensive statement before parliament broke up of what the government was going to do about it, because once parliament is not in session it is more difficult. And, if the situation does worsen, it might even require parliament to be reconvened.
We have not had that. The minister said a few moments ago that the government is going to do everything it can to prevent the situation from worsening. He has not been able to give us much evidence of what has been done, but the government is going to do everything it can to prevent the situation from worsening. Naturally we would support any move that the government can or will make to that end but, Mr. Chairman, the situation has already worsened when compared with what it was at this time last year.
It is as bad as it was in 1958.

Last night the minister told the committee-and I quote from Hansard at page 7254-in answer to a question of mine: Mr. Chairman, I certainly hope the situation will be much better than it was in the last two winters.
I was talking about the unemployment situation during the winter time. On what does the minister base that hope? This morning he has told us that the situation is serious in terms of unemployment, and it certainly is likely to get more serious as the autumn and winter approach. He said this morning-and we all hope, of course, that the situation will be much better this winter than it was during the last two-that the situation will be much better this winter. I should like to know whether the minister can tell us on what he bases this hope. There must be something in his mind which justifies this somewhat optimistic conclusion, at 79951-0-460	[DOT]
Supply-Labour
least an optimistic hope, that while the situation is serious

and I know it is more serious than it was this time last year-nevertheless he hopes it will be much better than it was during the last two winters. That is the short run position and the problem we must cope with at the present time is the short run problem.
While I am on my feet I should like to remind the minister, if he needs any reminder, that the long range problem is just as serious, just as complicated and just as difficult. During the decade 1950 to 1960 one million jobs were added to the economy of this country. During the decade 1960 to 1970, if this country is to approach or maintain anything like full employment, we shall need two million jobs. Now, we have the short run situation, which is serious. We have the long run situation, which is serious. In so far as the former is concerned the minister hopes it will be much better than it was during the last two winters. Can he give us some information on which we can share that hope with him?

It is quite obvious, Mr. Chairman. I am hoping that with the measures I have already announced and with the measures which we shall undertake, we shall alleviate the situation this winter and it will be much better than it was. It is on that that I base my hope, and I have every right to do so.

It seems to me that the hon. member for Vancouver East has put a very important question. The minister says he is satisfied, that if we have an unemployment situation comparable to last winter, the program of the government will be capable of providing jobs for all who need jobs. The minister will certainly agree that he is straining logic when he makes that statement, because all that the winter works program was able to provide was some
51,000	jobs. The government through the minister is not serious when it suggests that the three measures that represent its present program are capable of providing work for the numbers who have been out of work during the past winter.
That being so, what is the answer to the question put by the hon. member for Vancouver East? If in the month of September or October the number of unemployed rises to the level of the corresponding period last year, what program will the government resort to in order to provide jobs for those people who are out of work, recognizing that the present program, on the basis of the experience of the last two years, has not been able to provide a substantial number of jobs?
The government has said it is considering other plans. When are those plans to be put

Supply-Labour
forward? When are the programs based on those plans to be realized? Are we to wait until next winter? Is that the situation? If that is the situation, the minister can tell us. But what is going to happen to those people who are out of work? The government, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, cannot bring forward those plans without the approval of parliament. Parliament has to pass the necessary money; and the government must give the committee an indication if it will call parliament together in the fall, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, to authorize it to embark on the programs which the minister says it is now considering.
The minister has not touched on this phase of the problem at all. Of course it is not the only phase that he has ignored in this discussion. It is another question which has to be answered, if we are to feel that we have discharged our responsibility with regard to the request of the government that we should pass this particular estimate and the other estimates of the Department of Labour.
I listened to what the hon. member had to say, and I think I have answered practically all the questions time and time again, so I have nothing further to add.

Mr. Chairman, I have come to the conclusion that the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Vancouver East are hardly being fair to the minister, because it is quite evident that the government has no program, is planning no program and intends no program, and that the unemployed are to be treated in exactly the same way as the western farmers are being treated by this government.

There is one point that does disturb me. I am quite prepared to accept the word of the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister that studies are now being undertaken with a view to giving further consideration to the unemployment situation, and through that consideration plans for greater employment. A few minutes ago I asked the Minister of Labour about the financial end and his answer was that is a matter for the Minister of Finance.
Quite honestly, 1 do not believe that is something the Minister of Labour can expect us to swallow. If the government does have something in mind the Minister of Labour obviously knows the plans they are considering, and surely he must have been in communication with the Minister of Finance as to how that is going to be financed. He must know how they are going to finance something in the future. I think we in this house have a

right to know how they are going to do it if the House of Commons is not in session. My understanding is and always has been that the House of Commons and the Senate are the only bodies that can authorize the expenditure of money.
Now, I presume the plans of the Minister of Labour must involve the expenditure of federal funds. Can he tell us, because he must know, how the financial angle is to be handled and how, when those plans are at the point of being promulgated, the government is going to obtain the authorization of the House of Commons to do those things? Is there going to be a special session of the House of Commons or is it going to be done under authority of order in council, anticipating that at the next session of parliament a supplementary estimate will be passed? Surely this is one of the simple questions that should be asked by a member of the opposition. I hope the minister can give us a little more detailed reply than he gave to my question a few moments ao.

I do not know what particular financing the hon. member has in mind or what particular project he has in mind when he is so worried about financing. Let us take, as an example, the municipal winter works program. This is being financed by a supplementary estimate which will come before the House of Commons possibly during the next session of parliament, at which time parliament will be asked to approve it. An announcement was made in that respect. There will have to be a supplementary estimate for the additional cost of training the unemployed workers. This will be brought before parliament at the next session. Whatever the projects are, so far as I know at the moment, whatever the projects may be which will be approved, an announcement will be made and there is no doubt but that the proper method of financing will be used in that respect.
In other words the governor general in council can use a blank cheque in connection with a policy about which this parliament knows nothing.

I wonder if the minister can tell us how many, if any, of the members of this economics and research branch are working on the committee that was set up some five months ago to try to find a new method of measuring unemployment?
There are two members.

May I ask the minister whether this committee has completed its work, and whether the Department of Labour representatives on it have reported to him

in regard to that work? 1 ask this, Mr. Chairman, because it is obviously a matter of interest and importance to this committee, when discussing labour estimates, to have before it the work that has been done in this field. It would have been of great assistance to us if that work, which has been going on now for more than five months, could have been completed so we would have the report before us.
I know that the measurement of unemployment is not nearly as important as unemployment itself, but in order to assess the problem it is useful to have the proper statistics. There is a great deal of controversy now on this subject. This committee was set up for this purpose, and it has been working now for many months. Can the minister indicate whether there is any likelihood that we will have a report from him, during the discussion of these estimates, on the work of the committee?

I am advised that the work of the committee is nearing completion, and that they expect to write their report and make a report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to me during the latter part of next week.

I think it is very unfortunate that a report of this importance, which has a direct bearing on the consideration of these estimates, will be made to the minister concerned a few days after we have finished the discussion of these estimates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You still have trade and commerce.

Yes, we still have trade and commerce, and perhaps the minister will take up the matter with his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce to assure that when those estimates come before the committee we might have that report.
There is an interesting paragraph about this problem of the assessment and measurement of unemployment in this labour research bulletin to which I have already referred, which indicates that our present methods are not very satisfactory. We know that, because if they had been we would not have set up this committee. There are two procedures followed at present. One may result in the setting of a figure for unemployment which is too high, whereas the other may result in a figure which is too low. In commenting on this the labour research bulletin had this to say:
The government figures give people without jobs and seeking work as a percentage of the labour force. This is not the same thing at all. The labour force includes not only wage and salary earners and the unemployed, but also employers, own accounts (the self-employed) and unpaid 79951-0-460J
Supply-Labour
family workers in a business or on a farm. In 1959, these people averaged over 18 per cent of the Canadian labour force, so that the difference between labour force and labour supply was substantial. To measure unemployment against a conglomerate mass of workers, employers, the selfemployed and unpaid family workers is really not sensible.
Then further down it goes on to say:
So the sensible thing to do is measure unemployment against the total of "paid workers" (the neat d.b.s. term for wage and salary earners combined) plus the unemployed.
That seems to me to make sense. I think that is in accord with the international labour office method for the measurement of unemployment, which we have not adopted in this country but which perhaps this committee may recommend. If that does make sense, Mr. Chairman, it shows that unemployment, as a statistical measure in this country, is even more serious than one would gather from the dominion bureau of statistics figures given to us from time to time.
You are comparing apples and oranges to arrive at that conclusion.

That is what some of the unemployed cannot buy, apples and oranges. I feel that our discussion on item 165 and the previous item amply demonstrates why some members in this house thought it would be preferable to adjourn in June and come back in September, at which time the committee could have considered any proposal this government had in mind with regard to unemployment. This proves that we were right in making that suggestion.
I should like to ask a question of the minister under this item 165. If my memory is correct, and I think it is, the last information the Department of Labour issued on the number of those who were seeking employment in Canada indicated that there were 124,000. I think it said there were 124,000 who had been unemployed for four months or more. In view of that information, available to and supplied by his department, I should like to ask the minister whether, under this item for the economics and research branch, any special study is being made of the problem of those who have been unemployed for many months-I refer to the 124,000 for four months or more-as to the particular trades or professions in which they have been trained, with the idea of evolving any proposals to take care of that situation.
What I have in mind is this. Among that
124,000	is there any particular group or are there any groupings of trades or professions, and is any kind of research being undertaken with regard to them in an effort to try to solve the problem?

Supply-Labour
We have not that information here at the moment. We can check and see whether we can get that information.

It is not so much a matter of wanting a break-down; what I want to know is this. You have that problem of 124,000 out of those 300,000 applicants, I think it was according to the last statistical review. Is any special study being made by the minister's economics and research branch as to whether they break down into certain trades and professions, with a view to taking some remedial action?

I am told they are not certain whether there is any special data pertaining to these people mentioned by the hon. member, but generally speaking, on the whole manpower situation, our economics and research branch are continually studying and assessing the various categories.
I should like to ask this question. If any data are available, are they mostly of a trained or untrained classification? I am referring to the 124,000.
I am told that we can check on the matter right away. However, at the moment that information is not available to me.

Mr. Chairman, this seems to me an appropriate moment to make a suggestion that I have been turning over in my mind since the minister answered the Leader of the Opposition about this attempt to reconcile statistics, and the report of this joint committee on the matter. While the minister has said that this report may be available in time for consideration of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, it seems to me that procedure would not really be satisfactory to the committee for this reason. The Department of Trade and Commerce is merely the vehicle through which the bureau of statistics reports to parliament, but this is the department that has some responsibility in the matter. Particularly in view of the need for the minister to wait for certain information asked for by the hon. member for Vancouver East, it seems to me that the most suitable way of meeting this problem would be to have the minister let this item stand and go on with the rest of his estimates. Then at the end of the committee of supply, after all the other departments have been taken up so there will be a maximum amount of time to get this important document or this essential information and for all members of the committee to study it, we could resume the consideration of this particular item. I ask the minister to consider that suggestion.
You would then want it held until the government could consider it?

On that point may I say that I do not think it is a matter of the government considering this document. I would think both departments would welcome all the criticism of the document they could get before they decided to scrap the existing statistical basis and adopt a new one. I am making a serious request to the minister. At the same time I should also like to ask him a question about this study. I should like to ask him whether the committee, in its studies, have consulted Mr. Arthur MacNa-mara, who has perhaps greater experience in this field than anyone else in this country and who has, of course, a continuing connection with the minister's department or with a certain organism of the government connected with the minister's department.
He is chairman of the unemployment insurance advisory commission.

Yes; he is chairman of the unemployment insurance advisory commission and, as I happen to know, he has extremely strong views on this question. I should be greatly interested in knowing whether he has been consulted in the course of this study.

In answer to the hon. member for Vancouver East I want to say that I am now informed that these categories he mentioned are mostly untrained, but no specific data is available on the occupation characteristics of those who are unemployed for more than four months.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 165 carry?
Can the minister indicate what he proposes to do about my request?
What was your request?

The suggestion I made to the minister was this. In order to enable the committee to consider this report and to do so in the context of the minister's department, where it should be considered rather than under the Department of Trade and Commerce, my suggestion was that he should allow this item to stand until all the other business of the committee of supply has been done and then have it called. By that time, if his prognostications are correct, the report should be available to us. The other question which he might answer at the same time, is whether or not Mr. MacNamara was consulted by the committee.
What if the report is delayed?
In that case it could not be considered.

In answer to the last question, as to whether Mr. MacNamara was consulted, may I say that the answer is no, according to members of the committee. As to the first part of the request, the answer as far as I am concerned is no, because these are the same tactics that were adopted by the hon. member last year.

Really, Mr. Chairman, I think we deserve a better answer than that. I was not speaking just for myself. I was speaking for my friends on this side of the house; I refer to the official opposition in this House of Commons. I do not think this is an answer that the minister would like to leave on the record unmodified, namely the suggestion-and after all, it is unparliamentary-that these were the same tactics I used last year. There is an implication in that answer, and it is contrary to the rules to attribute motives.
However, I am making nothing of that matter. What I am saying is this. The request I made was made two years ago, as I think the minister will find, not last year. As the minister will recall, I made a reasonable request at that time. I requested that we should let one item stand until the winter works program was announced. What happened? The then house leader, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Prime Minister, when asked formally by my colleague the hon. member for Laurier, all refused that reasonable request.
When was the winter works program announced? It was announced in September. Where was it announced? It was announced at a provincial Tory convention in the province of Saskatchewan. Mr. Chairman, this item covers the administration of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. As I mentioned in my remarks last evening, I should like to remind the minister that when his estimates were under discussion last year he stated on May 15 that during the present session this act would be amended. I made a detailed study of the possible amendments. I felt that because of the far-reaching effects they may have on the lives of many thousands of Canadians, this matter necessitated an even more intensive study. This I am proposing to do; and in this course of action, I might say to the hon. member, the Canadian Labour Congress concurs.

Through the auspices of the commonwealth parliamentary association and the House of Commons I had the opportunity last year of visiting Australia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaya, Israel, Pakistan and the United Kingdom. Within a few days of my return to Vancouver, after an absence of three months and based on discussions I had with industrial and political leaders throughout the world, I made a speech for which I have since been condemned and commended. I said that I felt it was my responsibility to say that I thought Canada was facing a serious crisis in the months and perhaps the years ahead. I said if we were to maintain our standard of living and our competitive position as an exporting nation, there would have to be greater co-operation and collaboration among labour, industry and government.
I retract not a word of my speech made last December following my trip. Circumstances unfortunately have borne out the correctness of my statement. I say unfortunately, because there have been developments in Canada since that time which amply demonstrate the correctness of my conclusions. We face serious unemployment in Canada today and perhaps the problem will be more acute in the months and years ahead. We face increased competition from abroad, and threats of economic combinations. We are confronted with the possibility of cold war such as we have never before witnessed.
I therefore feel there is now an absolute necessity to have co-operation and collaboration among labour, management and government in the interest of all the people of Canada. Unless there is that co-operation and collaboration, critical as the situation may seem at the present time, conditions can get worse, and no one in this house or in Canada wants to see conditions get worse. I feel so strongly on this matter that that is the reason I rose.
I am not retracting one word I said, popular or unpopular though it may be. We
Supply-Labour
have to face major responsibilities in these critical times. We have to recognize, as I said yesterday, that automation is marching onward. We have to recognize-and I think this is of the utmost importance-and I am afraid too many in labour, management and government do not, that we are no longer in a seller's market; we are in a buyer's market. Since we are in a buyer's market, the interests of Canada demand a social consciousness on the part of all people. They demand that one segment of the economy shall not damn everybody else for everything that is wrong; and I apply that, sir, to government, management and labour.
I said when I returned last summer that one of the greatest needs, if labour and management could not get together, was for government to take the initiative in bringing them together. Government should take the lead within our capitalistic economy because, although I am a socialist and want to see socialism, I am a practical socialist and the practicality of socialism is ham and eggs on the table tomorrow morning for everybody if they like ham and eggs; if not, whatever they like or desire.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, although you may have thought I was out of order I am not, because I wanted to make those remarks as an introduction to a question on this item. I notice that the last part of item 167 has to do with the promotion of labour-management co-operation. Will the minister give us the fullest possible explanation of what, through the medium of his department, is done in the realm of labour-management co-operation; not only what has been done by the money expended in the past but in particular what will be done, the activity and the policy, in the fiscal year to which those estimates apply.
I know I am very often guilty of repetition, but I do want to reiterate that in my personal, and I will say humble, opinion we have now passed the time when government, with the knowledge and reports it should have; industry, knowing the competition they are now facing in a buyer's market and not a seller's market; and labour, that must have employment in order to live, have to get together and put their cards on the table- when I say that I mean it-and not completely condemn or damn each other, because undoubtedly there are mistakes on all sides. They should not try to find excuses, but should put the cards on the table so people can be employed, so they can produce and either consume or sell the produce so that government can function and meet its responsibilities.

This is the only item I know of under which the government can take a greater initiative in trying to bring about co-operation and understanding. If I say any more it will be repetition. I hope I have said enough to show how seriously I view this situation, and how important I think it is that on the initiative of government, management and labour relations should be improved. Would the minister be so kind as to say what is planned in so far as the government and this particular section of his department are concerned to bring about something which I maintain is absolutely necessary and long past due? Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver East for his contribution in respect of this vote, because I think it is very worth while. This is a matter that is in the minds of a great many people who have this interest at heart. I must confess to the hon. member that it is a very important matter in my own mind. What has been done in connection with this vote has been only on the plant level. We have helped in every way we could to organize committees on this plant level to promote efficiency in operation, reduce waste, promote safety measures and accident prevention. There are some 1,582 committees that we work with at that level for this purpose, but I think that is not enough. I think labour, management and government in fact should go beyond that. I want to thank the hon. member and assure him that this is also uppermost in my mind, to see what can be done in that sphere.

Mr. Chairman, I also listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who has so much knowledge of and interest in this field and who has expressed that interest and knowledge inside and outside this house over the years. I agree with him that industrial disputes which lead to strikes and the interruption of work are too expensive in our economic society to be tolerated if anything can be done to prevent them. They are wasteful; they impose a burden on the cost of production of goods in Canada at a time- and my hon. friend has said this-when that burden may prevent us developing our export trade and meeting the competition of other countries, and thereby prevent us from giving the kind of employment which we all want to see in this country.
I mentioned last night that employment in manufacturing is not as relatively important

in our economy as it was, but is still responsible for one out of every four jobs in Canada. Therefore we cannot afford this kind of thing any longer, any more than we can afford not to have a trade union movement as the basis of collective bargaining to prevent industrial disputes. The procedure for the purpose, of preventing industrial disputes, as the minister has said on more than one occasion, can be improved, can be made more effective, can be modernized, can be brought perhaps into a closer relationship with the industrial and labour situation at the present time.
The minister told us two years ago that he was going to amend the act. He has now told us it is such an important matter that more time is required. However much time is required, I hope those steps will be taken in the next session at least, and that we shall pass amendments to this legislation which will help the country to more effectively deal with this problem than has been the case recently; though I do not think we have too much with which to reproach ourselves in this country. Certainly our record is not perfect, but it is not nearly as bad as that of some other countries. In any event, we must improve on the present industrial relations disputes mechanism to make co-operation among labour, management and government in the settlement of such disputes more effective. No mechanism alone, however, is going to improve this problem. It is a problem which requires the exercise of wisdom and self-restraint on the part of all the elements in our society which are affected.
Some months ago I read, and perhaps the minister did too, a paragraph in a British white paper on the economic implications of full employment. It was presented by the United Kingdom Prime Minister to the parliament of that country about a year ago. There is one section of that white paper which deals with conditions of price stability, and it is a paragraph that seems to me to have a bearing on the whole question of industrial disputes. It reads as follows:
... If the prosperous economic conditions necessary to maintain full employment are exploited by trade unions and businessmen, price stability and full employment become incompatible.
This may seem to be labouring the obvious, but we do not always, in our economy, understand the obvious or perhaps we do not always act on the obvious. It goes on to say:
The solution lies in self-restraint in making wage claims and fixing profit margins and prices, so that total money income rises no faster than total output. In the absence of such self-restraint, it may seem that the country can make a choice-albeit a painful one-between full employment and continually rising prices, or price stability secured with some danger to the level of employment that might otherwise have been achieved.

On this subject of industrial disputes and how to improve our present procedures, I read the other day a very interesting article in a magazine called Saturday Night. The article was entitled "Common Sense Laws to Prevent Strikes" and was signed by somebody called Frank Howard. I wonder whether this is our colleague in the house, the hon. member for Skeena, although there is no implication to that effect in this article. If it is not the hon. member for Skeena I should apologize-
Why should you apologize?

I apologize for attributing to him an article, even if it is sensible. I should not give him credit, even for a good article, if he did not write it. This paragraph begins:
When labour goes on strike, or management resorts to a lock-out, there is only one way to settle differences-apart from government imposed arbitration.
Perhaps I might interpolate here that government-imposed arbitration, which perhaps is essential in certain emergencies, should certainly be restricted to a minimum; because compulsory arbitration by government will inevitably lead to government intervention and finally government control of the business or industry in which the government has arbitrated. Then he goes on to say:
The two sides must get together and talk out their differences. It is at this point that we need drastic changes, both in the law governing industrial disputes and in the procedures we have set up to handle these disputes.
Then he proceeds to recommend some changes. I would be interested, if the minister saw fit to comment, in hearing his observations on some of these changes that are recommended in this article by Mr. Frank Howard. I am only going to pick out some of the more important ones, at least the ones that seem important to me. He says:
First, we should eliminate the use of conciliation boards, even though they have effected some settlements. Their work is repetitive of that of conciliation officers.
Then he goes on to add:
At the moment, time and lack of authority handicaps the conciliation officer and restricts him in his efforts to assist the disputing parties. We should give him the power to arrange meetings of the two parties and the right to ensure attendance at such meetings.
In other words he would eliminate the board and exalt the importance and authority of the conciliation officer. Then he says this:
A time limit should be set within which each party should indicate to the other and to the Minister of Labour whether it intends to accept or reject the recommendations of the conciliation officer .. . Following this, and if rejection is made by either party, a strike or lock-out vote should be allowed.
Supply-Labour
Then he goes on in connection with this procedure by making this proposal, which I think is both interesting and important.
The strike or lock-out vote must be by secret ballot.
He has a good deal to say about the use of the courts and judges in the conciliation of industrial disputes. I should not have said "the courts"; I should have said judges. He says:
More and more as union-management relations have developed we have seen the entry of judges of the courts into those relations. Judges are schooled in the ways of jurisprudence. Their lifetimes are spent in dealing with words and the interpretation thereof.
I would suggest that a section of the court be established to deal with questions of interpretation of, and disputes arising out of, collective agreements. But, the activities of such a labour court should be confined to dealing with grievances and must not be extended to the field of negotiations.
He then says:
If two parties to a collective agreement want to name a permanent arbitrator then they should be allowed so to do and should not have to take their differences to a particular person or place for an adjudication.
This is an interesting article, especially if it should be an article written by a member of parliament, and it puts forward some constructive suggestions which no doubt will be considered by the minister when he is working on the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. If he would comment on some of these points I have put before the committee I would be glad to hear his views.
First of all may I say that I do not believe this Frank Howard is our colleague.
May I just intervene, then, to withdraw, ex post facto, any reference to the hon. member for Skeena.

Some of the things he suggests in the first part of this article have been in effect in the federal jurisdiction for many years, and with some success. The same suggestions have been made by other people in the provincial jurisdiction but not the federal jurisdiction. We have received no representations at any time from any of those affected by the federal Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act that conciliation boards should be abolished or the services of conciliation officers should be eliminated. Our experience has been that about three quarters of the disputes under federal jurisdiction have been settled by conciliation officers. They have performed very useful functions in this regard. The balance of one quarter of the disputes with which we have had to deal have been settled by conciliation boards.

I am not going to comment on what the experience has been in the provincial field; that is an entirely different matter. In these circumstances, and in view of the experience we have had, I feel that this is a good procedure. Certainly in my estimation anything in which success is to be found should not be thrown overboard by something else that may not be as thoroughly tested as is this procedure.
