There are other items that might be reduced, but at a time when there is so much unemployment, and particularly as some of it is seasonal, we ought to know why the reduction has taken place. The minister might tell us-
Will the hon. member allow me to answer one question at a time? I get confused when I get about three or four questions at one time.
I beg the minister's pardon.
It is a little confusing to me.
But the minister is sitting down. I do not understand.
I am getting the answer to the first question.
The minister is getting the information.
We have participated in an immigration hostel in St. Paul which now has been closed down because there is no further use for it.
Is that in Saskatchewan?
No, it is just outside of Montreal. The total cost was some $86,000. That practically takes care of the amount that is shown as a decrease under this branch.

Will the minister tell me what is being done pursuant to the vote on this item? The minister will understand that if seasonal unemployment is a factor, as the minister indicates and to the extent that he indicates in the present level of unemployment, this is a vote on which we should be given a comprehensive statement as to what is being done to combat seasonal unemployment.

This special services branch was organized in April, 1950 to handle projects which developed from time to time and which did not fall within the purview of the other branches. The main programs at present that we undertake are listed as follows: the federal-provincial farm labour program; the organized movement of workers between Canada and the United States; organization and development of the program to combat seasonal unemployment-I may say that is the do it now program-the municipal winter works incentive program. This branch also
Supply-Labour
acts as liaison with associations and employers in the various industries with regard to their manpower problems.

Since this is the item on which it is possible for us to discuss the winter works program, I would like to ask if the government gave any serious consideration to the suggestion which was put forward repeatedly by members of the official opposition, that instead of this 50-50 cost sharing basis some other formula should be devised more in keeping with the equalization formula for the payment of assistance to the provinces under the tax-sharing arrangements act.
As has been repeatedly shown by the hon. member for Gloucester, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's in speeches which I happen to recall earlier in the session, these winter works are concentrated mainly in the provinces which relatively need them the least, because they are the areas where the province can afford to pay its share. I think it would be interesting if the minister would tell us how many of the 55,000 jobs provided last winter were in the four Atlantic provinces, and how many were in Ontario.
What is the first question you want me to answer? Do you mind if I take them one at a time?
Not a bit. I will ask the factual question first, and it is this. Of the 55,000 jobs, if that is the right figure-and I do not know what 55,000 jobs mean-
That is incorrect; it is 51,000.

I beg the minister's pardon; 51,000. I would presume that a job for one day is a job and a job for three months is a job, but they are very different things to the person who has the job. It is really job-days which are significant, and if the minister could tell us how many job-days there were in Ontario and how many job-days there were in the four Atlantic provinces I think it would help us to see whether this program is really providing the most help where it is most needed.

The estimated number of man-days of work provided in Ontario totalled 539,075. The number of man-days of work provided in the province of New Brunswick totalled 55,100; in the province of Nova Scotia, 135,778; in the province of Prince Edward Island, 100 man-days and in Newfoundland, 18,166 man-days.
Perhaps the minister would not mind giving the figure for the whole country.

The estimated number of man-days of work provided totalled 1,938,839.

Supply-Labour

The next question I want to ask is this. The minister will certainly see that the number of man-days of work provided in the province of Newfoundland, which unhappily had relatively the highest level of unemployment of any province, is ridiculously small, to put it mildly. It is relatively a good deal smaller than the 100 days in Prince Edward Island, because in Prince Edward Island, because of the nature of the economy and the fact that the island is not very heavy industrialized, the unemployment was relatively not very great. But in Newfoundland unhappily it is relatively very great.
The minister will also see that the relief provided by this program in Newfoundland was very, very small indeed. It is for that reason, of course, that we put forward the suggestion that instead of paying a 50-50 share there should be some formula worked out dependent, in part at any rate, on the level of unemployment in the area, so that those areas with the highest level of unemployment, and therefore the least capacity to pay their share-
What kind of unemployment do you mean? Seasonal or traditional?

For the benefit of the hon. member for Edmonton West perhaps I should explain that I was talking about the winter works program, and presumably the government designed the winter works program to deal with seasonal unemployment. That is all I was talking about, and I was concentrating exclusively upon it.
It so happens that seasonal unemployment, taking one year with another, in the province of Ontario is relatively less, I think, than in any other province of Canada except possibly Prince Edward Island. It just happens to be one of the facts of life which we have to face. In other words, the seasonal problem in Ontario is the least serious compared with any other province, notwithstanding the fact that one third, if I can keep in my head the figures the minister gave me, of all the money is paid to Ontario.
No; one quarter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is 30 per cent to 32 per cent.

My hon. friend from
Cochrane, who is better at arithmetic than I, says 30 per cent to 32 per cent. Even according to my rough reckoning that is not very far from one third, and I will let hon. gentlemen split the hairs if they want to. It will not alter the fundamental point I am making, that you have in Ontario one third of the money spent in the province best able to pay its own way and which has the least or relatively the least seasonal unemployment.

We do not think, having regard to the national character of this problem and the fact that this money is being paid out of the national treasury, that the 50-50 formula is a suitable one, and we put forward very strong views which the minister told us at the time we put them forward would receive careful study along with all our other suggestions. I would ask the minister what conclusion was reached after that study.

There is no such thing as a 50-50 formula. As a matter of fact this is not a cost sharing program with the provinces at all. This is a program which has been brought forward by this government to help in the municipal works program, and it was suggested by the municipalities themselves. Naturally we cannot deal directly with the municipalities because the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, so all our work in this field must be done through the appropriate departments of the provincial governments.
At least six of the provinces have also helped in this regard by contributing 25 per cent and in one case 30 per cent of the balance of the payroll costs of this municipal winter works program. So there is no such thing as a formula that is 50-50. It is a direct contribution from the federal government through the provinces to the municipalities to encourage them to do certain works in the wintertime in order to alleviate the unemployment in those municipalities; also to lessen the financial cost with which the municipalities are burdened with in regard to unemployment assistance and other matters.
The minister says it is not a 50-50 formula. Will the minister assert that there is any case anywhere where the federal government pays more than 50 per cent of the labour costs?
This is the only program.

The minister says it is not a 50-50 program, and I say that the minister and I do not talk the same language. After all, that is all we have responsibility for, what comes out of the federal treasury. My understanding of the winter works program is that the federal treasury pays 50 per cent of the labour costs-
Payroll costs.

Very well; payroll costs; the minister can call them anything he likes. But if they pay anything different from 50 per cent I would like to know. That is what I should like to know; if the federal government pays any other figure than 50 per cent. I say it does not matter whether the rest is paid by the provincial treasuries or

by the municipalities. The plain fact is that in certain provinces these works cannot proceed because the municipality or the province, or in many cases both, simply cannot afford to lay out the other 50 per cent plus all the other costs of the project. I say that we recognize this principle in the fiscal field -the principle of the proper equalization of these payments-and if the winter works program is to be spread relatively uniformly across this country and do good where it is most needed, a new costsharing formula is required. The minister promised us that the government would consider that-
I certainly did not.
I can turn up the pages-
Go ahead, turn them up.

-and show the minister where he talked about our constructive suggestions and said that every one of those constructive suggestions would be considered. If all he meant was the same kind of consideration that is being given to the western wheat growers' proposals, it would be simpler to tell people at the start that it was intended to do nothing about them. I should like to know whether the minister has really given any consideration to this matter. There are ministers in the cabinet from some of these provinces, and I would hope they have made very strong representations in cabinet council to see that a fair deal is given to their provinces and to the municipalities in those provinces.

I can tell the hon. member that no representations have been made by the municipalities or by the provinces on behalf of the municipalities with regard to the suggestion he has made. Only yesterday I read a letter from the president of the association of mayors and municipalities, who are most directly affected by this and who have not been reluctant about bringing forward suggestions; and no suggestion of this type has been put forward either by the municipalities which we are endeavouring to help or by the provinces with whom we are working.

I hesitate to intrude upon the time of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I should like to advance a suggestion for the consideration of the minister which is to some extent an outgrowth of the winter works program. I think it would go a long way toward dealing with this problem of seasonal unemployment and even, to a considerable extent, with the type of unemployment known as hard core unemployment.
Hard core and seasonal unemployment can be the consequence of failure to utilize most
Supply-Labour
effectively the reservoirs of resources, skills and knowledge which already exist. It can be proven, I believe, that in many areas unemployment is most severe where an imbalance of development is found; where primary industry is not supplemented by secondary industry; where a single industry, either primary or secondary, maintains an entire region. It is in these circumstances that very often we find the most severe conditions of winter unemployment occurring and where there is growing evidence, also, that continued long term unemployment is likely to occur. The problems, to a large extent, originate in the inadequate utilization of existing resources, skills and knowledge, and the solution must therefore lie, at least in part, in a more effective use of these elements.
If we consider the contribution of the Department of Agriculture, not only the federal department but the departments of agriculture of all the provinces as well, we find that diversification, together with increased production and efficiency, have resulted from study, experiment and advice flowing steadily from these departments to the farmers concerned. Where advice based on study and experiment has been heeded, improvement has followed; but where advice has not been offered, or where it has been given and gone unheeded, there is a history of decline. This is positive evidence that close co-operation between a department of government and the people connected with an industry can have a beneficial effect.
Today we have been discussing the winter works program. Part of its effectiveness has been because of the utilization of voluntary committees of citizens in communities throughout the country in co-operation with the Department of Labour, national employment service offices in various communities and other associations concerned. My opinion is that if we could combine the type of service which has been effective in the agricultural industry with the method of reaching the people who need help through the use of committees similar to the voluntary citizens' committees which are now at work, we might achieve some very effective results. The majority of government departments, through their specialized branches dealing with economics, marketing, scientific research and so on, possess immense stores of knowledge concerning all resources in the industrial, commercial and agricultural fields. To be of greatest value this knowledge must get into the hands of people who can use it in developing the economy. There has to be an interchange, a flow of ideas, from the government to the people who can put this knowledge to work.

Supply-Labour
The means of doing this at the present time seems to exist in Canada only to a limited degree. My suggestion is that this lack of facilities might be offset by the use of regional development councils. Councils of this type do exist in Canada now. They also exist in the United States. But there is no national program of development councils, no ordered program which would achieve this result of utilizing most effectively all the resources of knowledge of all levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Did I correctly understand ihm to say there was no national program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said there was no national program of regional development councils of the type I have suggested. They exist now in regions but their work is on a local rather than a national level.
I believe that the way we can achieve the best results from this all-embracing program would be to provide a means by which these councils could readily obtain all the information which exists in all the departments of government that might be concerned. I believe that the onus for creating these councils lies with the regions which require help, regions where economic development is lagging or is in a state of imbalance. The communities within a prescribed area would form a council embracing representatives of municipal governments, business, industry and labour and this council would apply to the responsible government authority for a study of the problems of the region.
This is why I feel that the special services branch might be the one most affected by an idea of this kind. The regional council would come to a special designated authority in government and ask that a survey of its resources be made to determine what steps and assistance could be used to bring about an elimination of this state of imbalance. The federal government would act as a catalyst in bringing together all the resources of specialized knowledge that would have an application to the problem of the region under study. 1 would assume that the federal government, acting as a catalyst, would also have to secure the participation and cooperation of all the provincial governments, because those bodies also have a tremendous store of useful knowledge that could be valuable in a scheme of this sort.
Perhaps I may be permitted to give a specific example to show how this plan might work if it was acceptable. For the purposes of my illustration let me choose
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke) .1
a region dependent on agriculture, forestry and tourism-and if hon. members closely examine this illustration they will recognize that its economic constitution parallels that of my own riding-with only a small proportion of secondary industry and that largely seasonal. This region would request a study of its deficiencies and its strength. Representatives of the Department of Agriculture, the new department of forestry, the Department of Labour and in this instance the dominion travel bureau would be assigned to meet with the regional development council that had been created in that area. In consultation with the council the strength and weaknesses of the regional economy would be very closely assessed. Out of this would come a series of meetings at which officials of the specialized branches of government would, through the council, bring to the attention of the region the knowledge that could be put to work in its development.
I feel that the primary function here is to stimulate the latent initiative of the people in the region, because so much of the solution of the problems with which we are faced must originate with the people themselves. Government cannot do it all. Therefore the people in regions that are experiencing difficulty must be shown what they can do. Their own initiative must be tapped. They must be given a clearer conception of what might be done and a better understanding of their own potential, as well as what might be achieved through their own resources and what types of outside aid might be most profitably sought.
The role of government as I see it is to reveal possibilities not previously realized, to provide counsel, to encourage and lead toward balanced development. This is not simply the responsibility of government alone but is a responsibility that should be spread through the entire community. This plan would serve to make readily available to the people in the region affected the knowledge they may need to help them realize their own potential.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with interest to the speech that has been made by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. As a matter of fact one wonders why more hon. members on the government side do not take part in this highly interesting discussion concerning this most important department.
Oh, oh.
We do not get a chance. You fellows talk all the time.

I would be very happy to hear the whip of the Conservative party speak on this matter, because the hon. gentleman represents a constituency like mine where there are many workers who are very much affected by this proposal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The greatest industrial expansion in the history of the riding is taking place right now.
That is interesting, because that is the riding where the greatest dislocation occurred when the Avro contract was cancelled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I invite the hon. member to read the last few issues of the Brampton Conservator the contents of which indicate that a tremendous industrial expansion is occurring in that area.
I am glad that my hon. friend recognizes that the measures undertaken by the former government led to expansion in many areas in Canada.
Oh, oh.
That is pure political humbug.

My hon. friend says "That is pure political humbug". No one should know better than my hon. friend what is humbug.
Under this item we have the opportunity of discussing the winter works program. The minister has sought to indicate by reading the letter of the president of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities that this group endorses the program in its entirety. If the minister intended to create the impression that this letter was an endorsation of the program in its entirety, I am sure he will now agree that such is not the case. Undoubtedly the program was welcomed by the association of mayors in our country, just as it was welcomed by every hon. member of this committee. The criticism levelled by those in this party and by the mayors of Canada is that, welcome as it is, the program is inadequate and incapable by itself of meeting the problem of current unemployment.
I submit to the minister that notwithstanding the refinements and modifications announced by the Prime Minister last Saturday, the government has not taken into consideration the points raised by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities at page 4 of the representations they submitted to the government in 1959. They observed that:
The difficulties arise consequent upon the inability of municipal governments to finance the high costs and carrying charges of urban renewal requirements and the requirements occasioned by rapidly expanding urban growth-The difficulties of municipal governments are more in the field of capital costs rather than in the field of annual operating and administrative costs.
Supply-Labour
This is the heart of the criticism, yet this program does not touch the matter of capital cost, which is the main concern of the municipalities. This program is one in which the government shares with the municipalities and with participating provinces to the extent of 50 per cent of the payroll. That is the extent of the assistance provided by the federal government. It is absurd to suggest that this program can be represented as a vigorous onslaught on unemployment.
The minister told the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate a moment ago that least year 51,000 men were put to work under this program, but we know that in the month of March or thereabouts, on the basis of the lowest figures there were somewhere in the neighbourhood of half a million people out of work, 55,000 on the basis of the dominion bureau of statistics figures.
Last Saturday the Prime Minister, of course, did not mention the 25-point program put forward by the Liberal party this session, all of which were referred to by the Minister of Labour as inconsequential proposals. One of them, No. 7, provided for the modification of this program to make it more acceptable to the municipalities, as recommended by the federation of mayors and municipalities. The Liberal party did not put forward anything constructive, said the Minister of Labour, but last Saturday the Prime Minister made an announcement containing some of the very recommendations made by members of the Liberal party this session.
The hon. member should be in Stratford.

Let me tell the hon. gentleman where he should be. He should be in this committee giving careful attention to this problem, because he represents a city where there are lots of people who are vitally concerned with the effects of a program like this.
They get on with it, too.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege arising from the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East concerning the attendance of the hon. member for Edmonton West in this chamber. The hon. member for Edmonton West is one of the most faithful attenders in this committee.
Whose privilege is that?

If I have offended the hon. member for Edmonton West or the hon. member for Wetaskiwin I want them to know I take it back. Of course the hon. member for Edmonton West is a very active attendant in this committee, and no one

Supply-Labour
complains about that. I am sure he is a very sincere and devoted member. What I was complaining about is that I would like him to be as attentive to this matter as he is in respect of his attendance in this chamber.
The government takes the credit for this program. It says that as a result of its contribution to it, this represents a vigorous program designed to take care of the unemployed of our country. It speaks as though it was responsible for most of what was done by this limited program. Let up analyse the representations made by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, and see how insignificant is the 50 per cent share of the payroll cost of winter works projects carried out by the municipalities. I refer to page 1 of the representations made by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to the government in 1959. Here is what that body says with regard to the break-down of contributions to the winter works program:
The estimated total costs (labour, materials, etc.) of the approved projects aggregated $81,375,000.
They are now speaking of last year.
It is expected that the direct payroll costs will mount to $27,358,000, toward which the dominion government has undertaken to contribute $9,279,000, or 17.6 per cent of the total costs of the works expected to be undertaken between December 1, 1958, and April 30, 1959.
In these very figures we have the answer, we have the portrayal of the limited character of the federal government's program with regard to winter works about which so much vaunting has taken place, particularly by the Prime Minister when he spoke to this nation over television on March 3 last. This winter works program, to the extent that it goes, is welcome; but it does not meet the problem of unemployment. We have the statement of the mayor of Ottawa with regard to the inadequacy of this program, which was made only a few days ago.
It should not be forgotten that this program, in so far as the federal government is concerned, covers only 50 per cent of the payroll. It does not make any contribution toward the cost of supplies, and it does not deal with many of the indoor projects, suggested by the Canadian federation of mayors. I ask the Minister of Labour if he will deny that 50 per cent of the labour payroll costs represents only about 10 per cent of the cost of a project. If that is the case, one sees more clearly the limitations of this program which the Prime Minister in particular refers to with such satisfaction, as a method of providing work for the large number of unemployed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Would the hon. member like an answer to the question he put? The municipalities themselves estimate that the percentage is 34 per cent, not the 10 per cent which he indicated.

My hon. friend says the 10 per cent is wrong and that it is 34 per cent? Will the hon. member explain? I referred to the statement made by the federation of mayors and municipalities and I quoted from page 2. Does my hon. friend recall what I said?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: These are the estimated figures that came in from the municipalities for individual projects.
It should be 34 per cent instead of what I read?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Thirty four per cent.

That is the estimated figure. If my hon. friend says that, I accept it. This is the first chance I have had in this house to congratulate the hon. gentleman, who comes from my county, on his appointment as parliamentary secretary.
It has taken a long while.

My hon. friend does not want me to make any comment on that. I was taking advantage of the first opportunity to congratulate a man for whom I have the highest esteem. I said I was advised that it was about 10 per cent of the cost. The parliamentary secretary corrects me and says it is about 34 per cent. I have here the statement made by the organization in 1959. It will be found on page 2, under the winter works program:
The prescribed range and nature of works eligible for payroll assistance restricted such works to outdoor construction projects. This consideration acts to the detriment of those municipalities located in the more northerly sections of the country where, depending on the severity of winter weather, outdoor construction costs can be 50 per cent higher and more than in other parts of the country ... the payroll saving costs to these municipalities is, therefore, much less than the face value of the 50 per cent federal sharing in such costs or of the combined federal and provincial sharing in those provinces which contributed a further 25 per cent or 30 per cent to the total payroll costs.
Therefore it cannot be argued that this program is one which fully satisfies the municipalities. It certainly is not one which satisfies the municipality from which I come; it certainly is not one which satisfies the city of Toronto, and it certainly is not one which satisfies the city of Ottawa. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out, the cities to which I have referred to are areas, where there is a greater capacity on the part of the municipality to bear its share of the burden. But in most areas,

apart from my own city of Windsor, which is one of the areas where we have and have had a persistent level of unemployment, the winter works program, because it exacts a heavy contribution by the municipalities, does not enable in those municipalities as ready an opportunity of participation as cities like Toronto and Ottawa, where the municipal revenues are higher.
It is pointed out also by the association of municipalities, that whatever benefits do exist in this program are perhaps in large measure cancelled out by the cost of interest on municipal loans. Many municipalities, in order to undertake projects, have had to borrow. In order to participate a municipality itself must be prepared to make a major contribution. The only way a major contribution can be made in the case of municipalities which do not have the resources is by seeking credit. Everyone knows that pursuant to the financial and fiscal policy of this government, credit has not been obtainable in the last two years, except under exorbitant and unusually high interest rates.
Under this vote we are given the opportunity of pointing out what are the limitations of this program, limitations which certainly had not been analysed by the Prime Minister in the announcement he made last Saturday and which went all over this country as though a very comprehensive approach was being made to the solution of the problem of unemployment. Under this vote there is something else the minister can tell us, namely what the Department of Labour is doing; because after all a large sum of money is being voted, or is being asked for, namely $500,000. Since unemployment to a large extent, according to the minister, is seasonal, what is being done by the government to meet this seasonal unemployment?
I recalled to the minister last night, the work being done in the United States on this aspect of the problem. With regard to the comprehensive report made by Senator Eugene McCarthy, the chairman of the joint congressional committee on unemployment, I may say that body went from one end of the United States to the other examining this problem. When I find that we have in this country a statement as meagre as that which has been given us on these estimates, compared with the exhaustive analysis and report made, and made public, in the United States, I wonder whether a full appreciation exists on the part of the government as to how serious this problem is. We have pockets of unemployment in our country that have persisted now for some time. Are we to go on saying that this society of ours can do nothing about this problem? Our society can
Supply-Labour
do something about this problem. Our society can do something if the government is prepared to take those steps which will at least permit it to make the proper assessment which, under this vote, should be made available.

May I ask, at the same time, if the minister will answer a question which I have in mind. It has to do with the position of a municipality which may desire to take advantage of the winter works program. Evidence has been given here last night and today that some municipalities may be most anxious to take advantage of these programs but may be caught because of their inability to put through the necessary plebiscites for loans to obtain the money. My question is this. Has the minister who is in charge of the winter works program given any consideration or sought the advice of the Minister of Finance concerning the possibility of applying or renewing an act, the title of which I cannot remember exactly, concerning municipal financial aid? I believe that under this act the federal government made certain moneys available to the municipalities at low interest rates. Has consideration been given, in relation to this winter works program, to applying this financial aid act which I believe is still on the statute books?

To my knowledge no consideration has been given to applying this particular act to which the hon. member has referred. However, I assure him that I will certainly look into it and take up the matter with the Minister of Finance.
In reply to the hon. member for Essex East, may I say that I realize how vitally interested he is in this problem of seasonal unemployment. From time to time he has expressed his opinions about it. I want to say to him that, so far as seasonal unemployment is concerned, in our winter works campaigns we have some 175 committees organized at the local level. These committees are organized to tie in with the local employment office activities. These committees are comprised of public spirited citizens from trade union organizations, management, women's institutes, service clubs, chambers of commerce and so on, as well as municipal and provincial bodies and governments. These are people of high calibre, outstanding citizens in their communities who are helping in our efforts to combat winter unemployment. Many useful suggestions have come from these bodies, and many have been implemented.
We have had some success in combating seasonal unemployment, although it is extremely difficult to give an accurate figure or measurement of that success. I want to

Supply-Labour
thank these people, on behalf of the government, for their efforts, which are put forward on a voluntary basis. I should like to extend the same thanks to the local radio and television stations and the newspapers which have donated freely of their time in connection with municipal winter works campaigns and the do it now campaign. We believe that as a result a great deal of this unemployment in the wintertime will be alleviated.

I should like to make one comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East. I believe everyone in this house feels, and indeed it has been said, that the Minister of Labour has been greatly concerned about helping in every way he can by the use of this particular program, under which 50 per cent of the cost of a special works program undertaken in the wintertime is paid for by the federal government. This program is of comparatively recent origin, and it was designed to meet special conditions. I would just point out to the hon. member what he seems to have forgotten entirely; that in complaining about more not being done he has forgotten to tell us which federal tax he would recommend raising.

My hon. friend asks me a question. I would not hesitate, if I had given the assurances which were given by the Prime Minister, to fulfil those promises to take every way possible of doing so even if it involved the implication in my hon. friend's question.
We in our group are in agreement, and we would point to the corporation tax and the capital gains tax.

There is one thing I should like to point out before this item passes. I have had a little bit of arithmetic done for me-I say "done for me" because I did not actually do it myself-in connection with this winter works program. I believe that the lowest possible level of unemployment last winter, even taking the dominion bureau of statistics figures for every month from December right through until April, was about half a million. This figure of 1,930,000 working days divided among 51,000 people, according to this arithmetic I have, means 38 days of work each. I do not say that to disparage what has been done, but merely to bring these things into their proper proportion. It does seem to me that before we inflate and exaggerate these things we should know what the facts are. The unfortunate fact is that if you take the number of unemployed in the areas where the burden

is greatest, you will find the number of days of work provided would be away below this figure.
I know the minister will say that when these works are performed they provide supplementary work in other ways, and that of course is true. Supplies are used and equipment is used. However, I would question very much, after two years of winter works programs, whether many of the winters works that have been done across this country under this program would not have been done anyway. That again is not to disparage them. It is desirable to encourage some of this work in the wintertime; there is no doubt about that.
However, I should be interested in being told this. Of course the minister can say that this matter is not within his competence, and he is right if he says that; because the decision as to the projects rests with the municipalities or with the municipalities and the provinces, and not with the minister. All he does is veto them if they do not come within his categories. I should be greatly surprised if any independent appraisal would show that many things were done under the winter works program that would not have been done anyway at some time during the year in which they were done.
Will the minister permit a question?
Does the hon. gentleman mean me? If he does, I am complimented.
Is the hon. member suggesting that the winter works program should be abolished?
No.
And that we make no contribution to Canadian employment?

I believe that vocational training is important to Canada, and I think it is particularly important at this time. We live in a large country, a country which is going through an acute transition stage toward becoming an industrial nation. I think it is fair to say we have reached some industrial stature even now, but I certainly believe the years ahead will show that we are capable of reaching a greater industrial stature than we have attained at the present time. In order to do this Canada will have to provide for those industries we have now and for those we will have in the future the type of skilled labour which those industries will demand, and we must do this not only to provide work for those who live in this country at the present time but also to maintain our exports, which provide jobs and a living for a large percentage of our population.
Industries as they go forward, whether it is a matter of improving old plants by automation or of introducing new processes, are going to require different types of skills, and I believe it is the responsibility of Canada to train young people so they may have the skills which industry demands. I know I am not in order when I say that I believe we are not spending enough in Canada on education generally. That, of course, is a matter for the provinces, but here is one

field of education where the federal government could play a very important part.

I think it is about time we spent a little to see that men may walk the earth in peace. I say again that we in Canada have not spent enough on education generally, though I recognize that this is not a field into which the federal government can inject itself.
However, here is one aspect of education in which the federal government can play an important part. Here we are as a growing nation faced every year with the problems of young people coming out of school and looking for employment, yet we spend only 4 per cent of our total expenditure on education for vocational training. There may be those who believe that all students should go through school and follow an academic course leading to the arts and professions and so on. I think nature has decreed that a large percentage of our people are equipped to do that kind of work, but nature has also decreed that there are those who are going to have to make their living with their hands. I believe we have large numbers of young Canadians who have great native talent, but it needs to be trained. We spend billions of dollars to refine our raw materials for our factories but we spend very little-four cents out of every dollar spent on education-to refine the human resources that will process these raw materials.

I should like to add a word before this item passes. I should like to emphasize once again the importance of this item to the economic growth of this country. The government should recognize that it is responsible for employment and should, therefore, make special representations to the provinces inviting them to take advantage of this offer in connection with vocational training. Under this program, as has been suggested, schools should be built to provide this vocational training. In too many cases the youth of this country leave the primary schools unprepared for anything but unskilled labour.
I am sure the minister would agree that if vocational training were given it would be needless for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to advertise in the Belfast newspapers for skilled workers to come to this country. I am pleased to note that the unemployment insurance commission has been cooperating in this program.
Before resuming my seat I should like to put on record a paragraph from page 14 of

the unemployment insurance commission report for the year ending March 31, 1959, which reads as follows:
Direction to vocational training-Direction of individuals to vocational training courses under various dominion-provincial agreements and to courses in training centres approved by the commission resulted in many people receiving training in occupations where demand for workers had exceeded the supply. During the year, a total of 4,510 claimants received unemployment insurance benefit while attending vocational training courses. This was more than double the number of claimants directed to training during the previous year.
My reason for placing this paragraph on record is to show that less than 1 per cent of the unemployed in this country are taking advantage of this opportunity to attend vocational schools. I think they should be induced to take advantage of this training. This would be one way for the Department of Labour to help in solving our unemployment problem.

The case for vocational training has been very well put this afternoon by a number of hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, who I thought spoke eloquently and beautifully on a serious and far-reaching problem and offered a solution which was constructive and which should commend itself to all hon. members of this committee.
I appreciate and commend the government for its new move to increase the federal participation in the joint training plan with the provinces with respect to technical training. However, I do not believe they have gone far enough. I think this is a half measure, and will not meet the problem that at present faces us. In any of these problems the most important thing to do is to face their magnitude. This is something the government has failed to do. This fact was patent both from listening to and reading the debates of the last two days. Unemployment in this country has reached the level of hundreds of thousands of people, not just a few thousand. Among these hundreds of thousands of people, particularly in the case of the male unemployed population, the level of education is unfortunately not great. I have not the actual statistics here with me; I wish I had. However, I was interested to note that the large majority of the male unemployed had a grade 8 education or less.
Here is a tremendous opportunity. Here is something which must be done. However, the government is not going to accomplish it by offering a partial payment to provinces which are going to take up the challenge. The provinces were here in Ottawa this week looking for extra financial assistance. They are already overburdened and overpressed. Unemployment may have been considered at one time to be a
Supply-Labour
provincial problem, but it is no longer that. It is a federal problem. The federal government has in fact, taken over, the main and primary responsibility for unemployment in this country, and the problem of technical training is directly and inseparably connected with the problem of unemployment. In this labour force there are hundreds of thousands of people who need additional technical training, people who need either new skills if they have been displaced by automation or a skill in cases where they have never been fortunate enough to receive adequate training in the first place. There is a tremendous opportunity for an investment along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West last night when he was suggesting investments which are self-recovering, or which put back into the national economy more than they take out.
In discussing this matter on previous occasions I have said that it is a problem of considerable magnitude which must be faced on the basis of that magnitude. The expenditure involved in order to meet this problem might, by the time it became fully in force, amount to $100 million or $200 million a year. It is that order of magnitude which is required, not an expenditure of $8 million a year in participating with the provincial governments. Nor can we expect the provincial governments to raise the extra money required so that through this joint operation the job may be done effectively. This job will be done effectively only when the federal government accepts the responsibility and pays the whole shot. There is no way around it. Under the present distribution of responsibility and taxing authority as between the levels of government, there is no other way in which the challenge can be faced. I therefore urge the minister to take another look at the problem, to re-assess it, to consider the magnitude, and to come back to the House of Commons with a recommendation which is worthy of the minister and worthy of the problem he faces. I can assure him that he will get a sympathetic reception from all parts of this chamber.
Vocational training is an investment which would return much to the Canadian economy. It is an investment which would return just as much as the program which was put into effect after world war II, when thousands of young people like myself had the advantage of higher education at the expense of the government. That program was part of a rehabilitation process, and that is what is required now, namely rehabilitation of people who are unemployed through no fault of their own.
Startling was the revelation recently that only one person out of ten in our unemployed

Supply-Labour
labour force has the skills necessary to accept the jobs offered. Statistically, what could be more startling? What could be more revealing in respect of the nature of the problem? The other nine people required more training before they can accept the jobs that are pres-sently available in our national economy. We recommend that something appropriate be done about this matter.
As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate has said on numerous occasions, it does not make sense that people drawing unemployment insurance should not be able to take advantage of the technical training at the same time. It is far better that these people should go to school in the wintertime and learn something which will enable them, once they return to the labour force, to be more productive, more happily and more usefully occupied.
This is a program that does not need long consideration. It does not need an advisory council. All it needs is a government with the courage and imagination to put it into effect. We hope the minister will give it the necessary consideration, will recommend it to his colleagues, and will have them recommend it to the House of Commons.

these estimates. It has to do with the position of employees of gold mines, and I was under the impression that this matter came under federal jurisdiction. It has to do with what is called compulsory aluminum dust therapy, which I understand is practised in all the gold quartz mines in Canada, which would include those under federal jurisdiction in the Northwest Territories. This is a matter of importance because of the experience we have had in the Porcupine gold mine area, and I am sure the same applies elsewhere though possibly not to the same degree because there are not the same numbers involved.
This aluminum dust treatment was brought about by the McIntyre foundation-I am not sure of the name-as a cure or means of prevention of the scourge of gold miners, namely silicosis. From the point of view of company compensation costs it may have worked successfully, because certainly the incidence of silicosis has dropped sharply since the introduction of this therapy. But since this treatment began the incidence of tuberculosis in the gold mining areas has increased threefold, and the incidence of carcinoma, which is a fancy word for lung cancer, has increased at a terrific rate and there are fears among the people involved in the mining industry as to whether there may be some connection between the increase in these dangerous diseases and the treatment they have been receiving.
Some work has been done in this connection, and from this work and study we find that the medical association of Germany has banned the use of this aluminum dust on human beings. The British medical association has said in regard to this particular treatment that it is at present in the stage where experiments could possibly be conducted on animals but not on human beings. Last, but not least, the United States medical association has said that the McIntyre foundation, which manufactures and sells this aluminum dust to all the gold mines across the country, is not qualified even to experiment in this field. Yet to my knowledge all the gold miners in the industry are forced to take this treatment whether they want to or not; the dust is blown ino the rooms when they change their clothes before starting a shift and when they come off shift. The treatment is forcibly applied to them, and they have no choice whether to refuse it or not.
The results of the treatment in its present state have not been proven one way or the other. I feel that if miners want to take this treatment voluntarily then possibly they should be able to do so, but I think it is wrong that the federal government should be implicated in any way, especially as medical associations in the United States,

Britain and Germany are not agreed that it is of benefit to the workers. In fact the evidence we have at the present time is that the contrary is true.
I feel that the federal government has the responsibility of seeing that a stop is put to this compulsory treatment of miners, at least until such time as we have some assurance from medical authorities that it is in the interest of the employees and not just a means of curing a problem as far as the companies are concerned by eliminating silicosis, while replacing it with tuberculosis and lung cancer which are not subject to compensation. I think this is a terrible thing, and I believe the federal government should ensure that they are not in any way responsible for the continuation of this practice that we see across this country.

I, like the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, am rather hesitant to intrude on the time of the front benches of the opposition, but there are a couple of suggestions I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee under this item.
I wish first to make an appeal to the minister and through the minister to the government for the inclusion of farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act, so these people may draw unemployment insurance benefits when they are out of work. At the

Supply-Labour
present time there are many thousands of labourers required on farms in Canada, and particularly in western Canada. This requirement will increase in the next three or four months by a very large amount, and people will not be available to fill the requirement. I suggest that the principal reason for this will be that these people will not take employment on the farms because they cannot get unemployment insurance stamps in their books.
A good many years ago the agricultural industry, particularly in western Canada, was able to fill its requirements for additional labour by young people drawn from other parts of Canada, and I think particularly from the maritime provinces, Ontario and Quebec. This was a very fine arrangement for western Canada, because we have in that area today many of those young people who came west 25, 30 and 35 years ago, liked what they saw, established themselves and are now some of our finest farmers. This is a practice which has ceased almost completely since the harvest excursions which took place in those years were discontinued.
To many of us, and particularly those in this committee who represent agricultural constituencies in the west, one of the most serious problems we have is the lessening of our farm population and, with the decrease in the population, the disappearance of what we commonly know as the family farm. In this debate a great deal has been said about self-employment and family help. This is very important not only to western Canada but to the economy as a whole, because it provides a good deal of employment. I am sure much is going to be said on these items with regard to unemployment and the numbers of unemployed. If the appeal I make to the minister and the government to make available to farm labour the benefits of unemployment insurance were acted upon, it would do very much over the next four months to decrease the number of unemployed in Canada.
In conclusion I suggest to the Minister of Labour that he give very serious consideration to my next recommendation. I suggest to the minister that the national employment service prepare a weekly list of job openings to be sent out to rural and small urban post offices so the people in those areas who are without work will know of employment vacancies which are available and can make application. This is not done at present because these people draw their unemployment insurance benefits by mail on a semi-monthly basis. They do not have an opportunity to learn about these employment opportunities. By the provision of these lists and their posting in the local post offices it would give our people

in the rural and small ui'ban areas an opportunity to make application for such employment as is available.

The front benchers of the opposition are delighted to have the backbenchers of the government intrude on our time to support policies with respect to the inclusion of agricultural labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act, which we in the opposition have urged for a number of years; so there is no need to apologize for participating in this debate, as we are delighted to receive their support in this connection.
Before coming to the core of my remarks, which the press gallery will probably consider parochial, let me say this is a serious thing. In association with other hon. members I have brought it to the attention of the government over the years. Farmers suffer a disability because when they seek help the workers want to make sure they will retain unemployment insurance stamps in the event they become unemployed. I have had this experience when on occasion I have had to hire a man for three or four hours. On this account opportunities for casual employment with farmers are lost. In association with the previous speaker I urge the government to give consideration to the representations made on the subject by many organizations, and particularly the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the federation of agriculture of British Columbia and the British Columbia fruit growers' association.
I do want to take this opportunity to express my appreciation of the good work undertaken by the regional staffs of the unemployment insurance commission and the employment service in Nelson and Trail. It is not easy to fill positions under these circumstances; it requires a great deal of patience, and owing to human impatience and human weakness on occasion, and sometimes human discourtesy, arising largely out of misunderstanding of the act or the regulations, very often we meet someone who really thinks the officers administering those acts in the local offices are trying to do them out of something, without realizing that the responsibility of the officer is to administer the law and the regulations. On that account I want to express my appreciation, and the appreciation of the labour organizations in the district, of the work that has been done throughout the years by the officers and staff of the Nelson and Trail regional offices of the employment service of Canada and the unemployment insurance commission.
I want to make a couple of other points. I do urge that every opportunity be given

the regional officers to visit the smaller communities. They have had more opportunity in recent years, but I know it is very difficult for them to get away on occasion because their work is centred in those two larger centres in the constituency I have the honour to represent. But I think it would be to the advantage of the administration and of the employers and employees concerned if these regional officers had an opportunity to visit the smaller communities periodically. I believe in these personal visits, they give them the opportunity to get closer personal contact with the employers, employees and members of the representative organizations in the small communities upon whom they depend to quite an extent for the efficient working of the act at some distance from the larger centre. I also suggest that they be given this opportunity in the winter months particularly when we, owing to weather conditions, sometimes get large numbers of men laid off rather quickly because of the depth of snow and climatic conditions which occur at 3,000 feet.
There is one other point on which I should like to touch. Once again I want to protest against two government agencies being responsible for employment placement; first the employment service and, second the immigration service. I think the national employment service should be the sole agency responsible for the placement of individuals in employment. Because of the way it is done under present conditions it causes considerable ill feeling and unnecessary ill will, and in my opinion it is most unfair.
